She made a face and moved away.

Useful.

The market was not blind.

A field piece that did something valuable could still be a terrible purchase if nobody could keep it doing that valuable thing.

I looked again at the ribs.

Three narrow.

One wide.

Something in my first life moved.

Not memory exactly.

Recognition before memory.

I had seen that spacing on a wall.

No.

On armor.

No.

A broken door frame in Red Fen, maybe.

I hated this part.

People imagined living twice would make memory clean.

It mostly gave me twice as many places to misfile things.

A man with a gray beard leaned over the felt without touching it.

"Valek piece?"

The guild man nodded.

"His?"

"Estate says."

"He used it on North Cut."

"Estate says."

"Heard it saved his arm."

"Probably why he kept using it."

Gray Beard laughed.

Then lowered his voice.

"Heard it broke Jeren's hand."

The guild man did not laugh.

"I don't have that in the estate record."

"Wasn't his hand."

"Then I especially don't have it in the estate record."

Gray Beard moved on.

I stayed very still.

Saved his arm.

Broke somebody else's hand.

That could mean almost anything.

A mason wearing a brace might have punched a coworker.

People remained people even around magic.

But the rib spacing bothered me more now.

I stepped away from the table.

This was deliberate.

The broad man with the blue cord had already seen me stare too long.

I inspected chisels.

They were chisels.

One had a mushroomed head that should have been dressed down years ago.

I inspected a plane.

The sole was warped.

I inspected the cracked wash basin.

Still cracked.

My performance of indifference was becoming expensive in dignity.

Someone beside me said, "You buying the basin?"

"Strong possibility."

He looked at the crack.

"Why?"

"I have enemies."

He moved away.

Excellent.

Second bell sounded somewhere beyond the roofs.

The crowd tightened around the rear half of the room.

I stayed near the wall where I had space for both crutches.

A woman in a dark vest climbed onto the low front step.

"House goods first. Field piece after lot twenty-two. If you're here only for the brace, don't crush my pot buyers."

Several people shifted guiltily.

I liked her immediately.

The first lots went quickly.

Pots.

Two lamp brackets.

The warped plane sold, proving markets contained mysteries greater than magic.

I watched bidders more than goods.

Guild-blue cord bought the box of chisels.

Account-case woman bought nothing.

Gray Beard disappeared before lot twelve.

Two work-coat men remained near the back.

One whispered numbers to the other.

Not treasure hunters, probably.

Trade buyers.

That mattered.

By lot eighteen my right hand wanted a break. I shifted to the wall, rested one crutch against my hip, flexed my fingers, then changed hands carefully.

No heroics required.

The auctioneer sold the cracked basin.

I felt betrayed.

Then she said, "Twenty-three. Registered impact brace from the Valek estate. Demonstration before bidding. Give Rusk room."

The guild-cord man was Rusk.

Good. One fewer nameless person in the world.

He cleared the rear table and brought out a thick square of timber already scarred from previous abuse.

Then a wooden practice arm.

That was sensible.

The arm had a jointed elbow, a leather-wrapped forearm, and a heavy base.

Rusk fitted the metal sleeve over it.

The brace closed with two ordinary straps.

No flash.

No hum.

The red stone stayed dull.

He positioned the practice arm over the timber block.

"Brace was demonstrated for estate registration three days ago," he said. "Same procedure. Same striking hammer. No claim beyond demonstrated function."

The auctioneer lifted a long-handled hammer.

The crowd gave her more room.

Smart crowd.

She handed it to Rusk.

He checked the brace once.

Then struck the practice forearm.

Hard.

The impact made half the room flinch.

The timber block jumped.

The practice arm did not break.

The red stone flashed once.

Not bright.

Deep red, almost black at the center.

The four ribs tightened.

I heard it.

A short metal click from each rib, not at the moment of impact but just after.

One.

Two.

Three.

Four.

My stomach dropped.

I knew that sequence.

Not the brace.

The sequence.

I had heard it under a gate in the first life while a man named Teren screamed at everyone to stop hitting the door.

We had not stopped hitting the door.

We had been twenty-three and extremely committed to solving problems with force.

The door had opened.

The wall beside it had also opened.

Later, much later, somebody explained why.

Catch ribs.

Load taken in stages.

Then held.

Or transferred.

Or something adjacent to both.

I remembered the argument better than the explanation.

Teren had called us animals.

We had objected because one of us was technically an elf.

Not useful.

I watched the brace.

The red stone faded slowly.

Rusk waited.

Nobody moved.

Then he struck again, lighter.

The brace took it.

This time the ribs clicked almost together.

Different.

I did not know why.

That was important.

The auctioneer said, "Demonstrated against two direct strikes. Estate makes no claim for side load, blade load, repeated field use, remaining service life, recharge, or repair. Opening at six copper."

Six.

My private wealth was in another building and insufficient by a factor I did not need currency conversion to appreciate.

A work-coat man raised two fingers.

"Six."

Account Case said, "Seven."

Guild-blue cord did not bid.

Interesting.

The second work-coat man said, "Eight."

The auctioneer looked around.

I did nothing.

Not because I was cleverly hiding my interest.

Because I had one copper.

There were limits to theatre.

"Nine," Account Case said.

The first work-coat man leaned toward the second.

Whisper.

"Ten."

That was already more money than anything I had personally purchased in this life by enough margin to change the shape of the thought.

And I still wanted it.

Not at ten because I knew its value.

I did not.

I knew one sound.

One rib pattern.

One memory of a door and a wall and Teren swearing at us.

That was not appraisal.

It was a direction.

The market knew the brace could absorb a hammer strike.

That alone was worth real money to masons, guards, breakers, anyone who liked keeping forearms attached.

If I was right about the rib family, the visible function might be the least interesting part.

If I was wrong, it was an old impact brace with no service shop.

Both possibilities were expensive.

"Eleven," Account Case said.

One work-coat man shook his head.

The other stopped bidding.

The auctioneer waited.

"Eleven once."

Rusk's eyes moved over the room.

For half a second they stopped on me.

I looked at the cracked basin's former spot.

There was no basin.

My acting lacked props.

"Eleven twice."

A voice from the doorway said, "Twelve."

Everyone turned.

A thin older woman stood just inside the door wearing a rain-gray coat despite the dry weather.

She had not been there for the demonstration.

Account Case frowned.

"Thirteen."

The older woman said, "Fourteen."

Immediately.

No hesitation.

That changed the room.

Account Case closed her mouth.

The work-coat men looked at each other.

Rusk watched the older woman.

I watched everyone.

Fourteen copper.

For a field piece with no current service mark and uncertain repair.

The market was not treating it like junk.

Good.

That would have been stupid.

The question was why the woman thought fourteen was acceptable without seeing the demonstration.

Maybe she already knew the piece.

Maybe she knew Valek.

Maybe she was an idiot with money.

All remained possible.

"Fourteen once."

No bid.

"Twice."

Nothing.

"Sold."

The older woman did not smile.

That annoyed me more than if she had celebrated.

The crowd loosened.

People immediately began talking as though they had all predicted fourteen.

I stayed where I was.

The woman went to the front to settle the purchase.

Rusk removed the brace from the practice arm.

The red stone was dull again.

I watched his hands.

He did not touch the stone.

He loosened the upper strap first.

Then lower.

Then, before lifting the brace, he pressed the wide fourth rib with his thumb.

A tiny click.

Not activation.

Maybe release.

Maybe habit.

Maybe nothing.

I knew how to check a catch assembly once.

Or I had.

You loaded a thread of mana into the first rib and watched where the return came out.

No.

That was for bridge locks.

For braces you touched the housing and bled current across the seam.

Maybe.

I could picture my own older hand doing something with two fingers and a copper probe.

I could not picture what happened next.

And current me could barely produce enough clean external effect under Hessa's supervision to rotate a marked strip once out of three tries.

So even if I remembered perfectly, which I did not, I was missing the part where the person performing the test had mana worth mentioning.

Useful limitation.

I waited until the older woman had paid.

Then I approached Rusk.

Not the buyer.

"That fourth rib," I said.

He looked at me.

"What about it?"

"You pressed it before removal."

His expression changed slightly.

Not alarm.

Recalculation.

"Unload check."

"Meaning?"

"Meaning I check it before I take it off the frame."

"Because?"

"Because I like my fingers."

That was a warning.

A good one.

I nodded.

"Fair."

He waited for the next question.

I did not ask whether the brace could hold force.

If he knew, I learned nothing by revealing why I cared.

If he did not know, I had just improved somebody else's appraisal.

Instead I said, "Who would service something like that if the original shop is gone?"

Rusk glanced toward the buyer.

She was still at the front table.

"Depends what it is."

"Tag says impact brace."

"Tag says what estate can prove."

I liked him considerably more.

"And if someone wanted more than the tag?"

"Pay an assessor."

"Any assessor?"

He snorted.

"Any baker can also make shoes."

"Badly."

"Exactly."

He started folding the gray felt.

I shifted one crutch so a departing bidder could pass behind me.

"Who reads old field hardware?"

Rusk looked at me again.

"You buying old field hardware?"

"I own one bad tool."

"That wasn't my question."

"Then no."

He smiled once.

Small.

"Mara Quill reads old housings and maker work. Doesn't certify combat use. Doesn't promise function. Doesn't touch bonded pieces."

A name.

Not a solution.

Good.

"Where?"

"South registry row, three mornings a week if she's there."

"Expensive?"

"Compared to what?"

I considered this.

"A cracked basin."

He stared at me.

"More."

"Tragic."

I left before asking too much.

Outside, the street felt wider even though the crowd had spilled into it.

I moved toward home slowly.

Fourteen copper.

The number did not feel impossible.

That was new.

It felt far.

There was a difference.

Early in this life, two copper had been an event because almost everything was an event.

Now I had paid two copper for a holdfast because I wanted the tool, spent bits on food and travel, missed a one-copper job because I had chosen to be five days east, and stood in a room where fourteen copper had bought something I might have wanted very badly if I knew more.

I did not need fourteen copper tomorrow.

The brace was gone.

That mattered too.

Money after the sale could not buy the sold thing.

I had spent most of my first life thinking about equipment after I needed it.

Then, once I had money, I had thought about equipment before I needed it.

That transition had been quiet enough that I had forgotten it was a transition.

Current me had one copper upstairs.

More importantly, current me had no reserve for surprise.

That bothered me.

Not because I was poor.

Because I had just seen what being unready cost.

At home, Tavi was in the courtyard arguing about gates again.

I passed without jurisdiction.

Lyssa sat near the window with dark cloth across her lap.

Still not the green vest.

She looked up.

"You bought something."

"No."

"You look like bought."

"I look like failed to buy."

"Worse."

"Much."

I went upstairs.

The copper sat where I had left it.

I looked at it.

One copper remained one copper.

Useful.

Spendable.

Not sacred.

Also not fourteen.

I took out the narrow scrap and wrapped charcoal.

Under the holdfast notes, I wrote:

OLD FIELD HARDWARE

MARA QUILL

SOUTH REGISTRY ROW

Then, after a moment:

RIBS 3 NARROW / 1 WIDE

RED STONE

UNLOAD CHECK 4TH RIB

14 C SOLD

I stopped there.

I did not write what the brace did beyond what I had seen.

Two hammer strikes absorbed on a practice arm.

That was real.

The four clicks were real.

My memory was not nothing.

It was also not enough.

I put the charcoal away.

Across the room, high above my clothes, the wrapped holdfast sat on sailcloth with its ring sideways and its warning tag visible.

DO NOT TURN RING.

Two copper.

Bought because I had seen enough to think it worth owning and not enough to trust it.

Maybe that had been the beginning of something.

Not collecting.

That sounded too clean.

Preparedness, maybe.

Optionality.

A bag of bad decisions with good reasons.

I liked the last one better.

Downstairs, Tavi shouted that somebody had moved gate.

I ignored him.

For the first time in several days, I had something more expensive to think about.

# CHAPTER 323

## THE HELD WEIGHT

The slab stopped falling three inches above a man's hand.

Nobody screamed until after.

That was probably why he kept the hand.

I had been halfway down Kiln Street, thinking about money in the vague and annoying way people think about a tooth they have decided not to touch, when six stoneworkers began moving a lintel across the road.

The lintel was gray, long, and large enough that ordinary men should have needed rollers, a cart, or a religious experience.

They had something better.

Maybe.

Two workers carried a black iron frame between them. It looked like a narrow doorway with no wall around it, shoulder high, crossbar thick, four short chains hanging from the lower corners.

The lintel hung beneath those chains.

Not lightly.

That distinction mattered.

The men still leaned into the load. Boots scraped. Shoulders worked. A third worker walked backward ahead of them with both hands raised, guiding the stone through the crowd.

But the lintel moved as if it weighed a quarter of what it should.

Maybe a third.

Enough less that six people could manage it.

Enough more that they were not pretending.

I stopped near a shuttered dye shop and gave them room.

Kiln Street narrowed at the bend. Everyone else gave them room too.

Carrow understood large stone.

The guide called, "Left corner. Left. Left. Hold."

The front pair adjusted.

One of the short chains clicked.

The sound was wrong.

I did not know the machine.

I knew that.

I also knew the difference between a working click and a load-bearing object asking to become a story people told later.

The guide heard it too.

His head snapped toward the left chain.

"Hold."

Everyone stopped.

The lintel dipped.

Not much.

An inch, maybe.

The black frame shuddered.

A brass disk at the top left corner went from dull yellow to white.

The worker under that side said, "That's not hold."

"Nobody move," the guide said.

Good advice.

Someone behind me tried to squeeze past anyway.

I put one crutch sideways across the gap.

"No."

He looked at me.

"I'm going around."

"Go around farther."

"I can fit."

The lintel dropped another inch.

He went around farther.

Also good advice.

The front-left worker had both hands on the frame. His right hand was near a small red lever fixed beneath the bright brass disk.

The guide saw it.

"Don't touch red."

The worker froze.

"Wasn't."

"You were thinking about it."

"I think about lots of things."

"Think quieter."

The rear pair laughed once.

Too sharp.

Fear laughter.

I knew that one.

The guide moved closer without stepping under the lintel.

He was a square man in a sleeveless leather work coat, dark hair cut nearly to the scalp, both forearms marked with old pale burns.

He stared at the white brass disk.

"How long white?"

The front-left worker said, "Just now."

"Before the click?"

"After."

"Sure?"

"No."

Excellent.

Nothing improved an equipment failure like uncertain chronology.

The guide looked toward a woman standing at the rear chain.

"Mera."

She shook her head before he finished.

"Don't ask me to bleed it."

"I wasn't."

"You looked at me in a bleeding-it way."

"Can you read the return?"

"From here? No."

That word mattered.

Return.

The same family of word I had been trying and failing to remember yesterday.

Not proof of anything.

A city contained more than one machine with a return.

Still.

I stopped thinking about fourteen copper.

The frame clicked again.

This time two corners answered.

Left front.

Right rear.

The lintel twisted.

The man at the front right moved automatically to catch the dropping stone.

I said, "Hands out."

So did the guide.

His version was louder.

"HANDS OUT."

The man jerked back.

The lintel fell.

Three inches.

Then stopped.

His hand had been under the edge a heartbeat earlier.

Nobody screamed until after.

The man stared at his fingers.

Then at the stone.

Then said, "Fuck."

That seemed correct.

The guide took one slow breath.

"Everyone still."

The brass disk stayed white.

The frame had not lowered with the lintel.

The chains had lengthened.

No.

Not lengthened.

They looked the same.

The stone hung lower because the left-front corner of the frame had rotated slightly inside its joint.

A load joint.

Maybe.

I knew better than to name things from across a street because they resembled things I had once broken.

The guide looked at the crowd.

"Need a wedge kit. Tan box. East yard."

One of the rear workers said, "I'll go."

"No. You're on the frame."

"We're all on the frame."

"Exactly."

He scanned again.

His eyes passed over me.

Came back.

Not because I was special.

Because I had already blocked the idiot from walking under the machine and I had two crutches, which made me visually memorable in a street full of people pretending not to stare.

"You mobile?"

I looked down at myself.

"Controversial question."

"Can you get to East yard?"

"Which East yard?"

"Kiln guild. Blue lintel over the gate. Two streets."

"Yes."

"Tell Jessa: Tan wedge box. South lift. White corner. Don't send a child."

"Why not a child?"

"Because they'll send the wrong tan box."

Fair.

I turned.

"Wait," Mera said.

I stopped.

She pointed at my bag.

"Charcoal?"

"Yes."

"Write white corner."

I pulled out the narrow scrap.

"On this?"

"Anywhere you won't improve the message."

I liked her immediately.

I wrote on the bottom edge beneath yesterday's notes:

TAN WEDGE BOX

SOUTH LIFT

WHITE CORNER

Then I left.

Two streets was not far.

It was farther when half of Kiln Street had decided to watch the almost-crushed-hand show instead of moving.

I took the outside edge, used a cart rut where the stones were flatter, and moved fast enough to make my shoulders complain without doing anything stupid.

The blue lintel was impossible to miss.

The East yard had a gate wide enough for stone carts and a painted board beside it:

KILN MASONS' COOPERATIVE

DELIVERIES EAST

PUBLIC COUNTER NORTH

I went east.

A woman behind a high table looked up.

"Public counter north."

"Tan wedge box. South lift. White corner."

She was already moving before I finished.

Good message.

"Who sent?"

"Square man. Burned forearms. Very committed to nobody touching red."

"Davin."

She shouted through a side door.

"Jessa! South lift went white. Tan wedges."

A voice answered, "Which tan?"

The woman looked at me.

I said, "He specifically said not to send a child because they'd send the wrong tan box."

She closed her eyes.

"Useful."

"I thought so."

Then she shouted, "FIELD TAN. SOUTH LIFT."

"That's different!" the voice yelled back.

"I KNOW."

A young woman came through the side door carrying a rectangular wooden case nearly as long as my thigh. Tan paint. Black corners. Two leather handles.

She took one look at me and handed me nothing.

Also good.

Instead she said, "Show me."

We went back together.

She moved quickly enough that I did not try to match her stride. I knew where she was going. She knew I had crutches. We could both survive twenty seconds without turning it into a moral lesson.

When we reached Kiln Street, nobody had moved.

The stone still hung three inches lower at the bad corner.

The white disk had dimmed slightly.

Davin saw Jessa and said, "About time."

Jessa said, "Fall on yourself."

Not warm.

Possibly affectionate.

Work relationships were difficult to classify from one sentence.

She set the tan case outside the drop line and opened it.

Inside were six black wedges, two hooked rods, a short mallet, and three flat pieces of pale stone with brass threads through them.

Not ordinary wedges.

Of course.

Jessa looked at the frame.

"Which corner first?"

"White."

"It isn't white now."

"It was."

"How long?"

"Long enough."

"Excellent measurement."

Davin pointed at Mera.

"She saw the return."

Mera said, "I said I couldn't read the return from there."

"Same difference."

"Those are opposite sentences."

Jessa ignored them both.

She crouched near the front-left leg of the frame without entering beneath the lintel.

One of the pale threaded stones came out of the box.

She pressed it against the black metal upright.

Nothing happened.

Then she moved it six inches higher.

The brass thread darkened.

She stopped.

Moved it lower.

Bright again.

Higher.

Dark.

"Load is sitting above the lower seat," she said.

Davin's face tightened.

"How much?"

"Enough that red would be stupid."

The front-left worker removed his hand from the red lever even though it had already been nowhere near it.

I respected that.

Jessa took a black wedge.

"Front right first. Then rear left. We take the live corner last."

Davin nodded.

The crew moved with irritating slowness.

Which was correct.

A wedge went between the lower frame foot and the street stone on the front-right corner. The hooked rod turned something I could not see. The frame clicked.

Nobody flinched this time.

Second wedge.

Rear left.

Another click.

The lintel did not move.

Jessa checked the pale stone again.

"Better."

Davin said, "Live corner."

"Not yet."

"Why?"

"Because I said not yet."

"Good technical explanation."

"You want the long one?"

Davin stopped talking.

I leaned on both crutches and watched.

This was not my machine.

That was becoming one of the more useful sentences in my second life.

I recognized pieces.

Not enough.

The pale stone was some kind of load reader, probably.

The wedges were doing more than holding the frame physically. The threaded brass in them responded when Jessa seated them. The black frame's weight changed subtly each time, not lighter exactly, but less eager to move.

I had used things like this.

Maybe.

Not this.

I remembered a siege engineer named Corl dropping a gate beam onto his own boot because he had insisted the stabilizers were "mostly mechanical."

They had not been.

His boot had become mostly flat.

That memory offered no useful specifications.

It did strongly support listening to Jessa.

She checked the live corner a third time.

"Now."

Davin shifted the crew.

"On my count. No lift. We are only taking slack."

The six workers adjusted hands and shoulders.

Jessa set the third wedge.

"One."

The hooked rod turned.

"Two."

The frame groaned.

"Three."

The brass disk flashed white.

Everyone froze.

The red lever jumped downward on its own.

Half an inch.

Jessa hit it sideways with the mallet before it could drop farther.

The lever snapped back up.

The lintel slammed down onto the three wedges.

Not far.

Enough.

The street shook under my right foot.

Someone screamed again.

This time because screaming was available.

Then silence.

The lintel stayed.

The black frame above it went slack.

All four brass disks darkened.

Jessa sat down directly on the street.

Davin said, "Good."

She looked up at him.

"I will kill you."

"After lunch?"

"Before."

"Scheduling problem."

The front-right worker started laughing.

Then Mera did.

Then everybody except Jessa.

Jessa eventually did too, which made it less concerning.

The crowd began breathing again.

Davin looked at the stone.

"Nobody moves the lintel until second frame gets here."

One worker said, "We can roller it."

"No."

"It's seated."

"No."

"We have six."

"Then six of you can stand here and admire it."

That ended that.

Jessa closed the tan case.

I had not touched anything.

This was also correct.

Davin looked at me.

"You ran clean."

"I moved aggressively. Running remains aspirational."

He glanced at my crutches.

"Fair."

Then he reached into a belt pouch.

I said, "No."

His hand stopped.

"No what?"

"If you're about to pay me for carrying six words two streets, no."

"It was seven."

"Then absolutely not."

He took out a small metal token instead of a coin.

Square. Black. Hole through one corner.

"Wasn't paying."

"Good."

"Yard chit."

I looked at it.

"Why?"

"Because you didn't improve the message."

Jessa, still sitting on the street, said, "Rare skill."

Davin held the chit out.

"Gets you through East gate if you need the public counter after deliveries start. Doesn't get you tools. Doesn't get you work. Doesn't get you into stores. Don't make it interesting."

I took it.

"You make a very compelling gift."

"Give it back."

I put it in my bag.

"Too late."

He looked mildly disappointed.

Good.

The worker who had nearly lost his hand was still staring at it.

Mera slapped his shoulder.

"Buy gloves."

"Gloves wouldn't help."

"Then buy better instincts."

"Where?"

"Public counter north."

I laughed.

Jessa stood and brushed stone grit from her trousers.

I nodded toward the black frame.

"What is it?"

Davin answered first.

"South lift."

"I gathered that."

Jessa said, "Old counterload frame. Cooperative owns two. This one is the worse one."

"Why use the worse one?"

"The good one is lifting a roof beam."

Reasonable.

I pointed with my chin toward the now-dark brass disk.

"White means?"

Jessa looked at me for a second.

"Depends how it gets white."

Good answer.

"Today?"

"Today it meant one seat stopped giving the frame somewhere safe to put what it was holding."

That was more specific than I expected.

"Holding weight?"

"Holding load."

"Difference?"

"Yes."

She picked up the tan case.

I waited.

She did not elaborate.

Also good.

Davin said, "Don't teach strangers the lift."

Jessa said, "I didn't."

"He's got the face."

I said, "What face?"

"The one where you think three questions becomes competence."

I considered objecting.

Then remembered the gate in my first life.

The wall beside it opening.

Teren calling us animals.

"Unfair," I said.

Davin nodded.

"Means I'm right."

He turned back to his crew.

The conversation was over.

That was fine.

I left before I became useful again.

The square black yard chit knocked lightly against the wrapped charcoal inside my bag.

Not money.

Not work.

Not an artifact.

Access.

A very small kind.

Yesterday fourteen copper had bought a dead mason's old field brace.

Today a cooperative-owned counterload frame had nearly eaten a man's hand while moving one lintel.

Both objects were expensive in ways I did not know how to price.

That was the part my old life had made easy to forget.

By fifty-nine, I had lived around institutions rich enough to own the strange things.

Guilds.

Companies.

Military stores.

City crews.

Adventuring houses with locked equipment rooms and quartermasters who could explain, at length, why whatever I wanted was not mine.

I had eventually owned expensive things personally.

Before that, I had used expensive things other people owned.

Those were different economic lives.

Current me had been thinking too much like every useful object had to become mine before it could matter.

That was stupid.

Not because ownership was bad.

Ownership was excellent.

I remained strongly in favor of it.

But a fourteen-copper brace and a cooperative lift frame were teaching adjacent lessons.

Reserve mattered.

Access mattered too.

So did knowing which person to listen to when a machine decided to become dangerous.

I reached the next corner and stopped under an awning to rest my hands.

The narrow scrap was still out.

At the bottom, beneath MARA QUILL and the brace notes, I added:

KILN EAST YARD

BLACK CHIT

COUNTERLOAD FRAME

WHITE != ONE THING

JESSA: LOAD NOT WEIGHT

Then I stared at that last line.

Load not weight.

I knew there was a technical distinction hiding in there.

I had probably known it once.

Maybe I still did somewhere inconvenient.

I did not dig for it.

There were enough people in Carrow who knew things now.

That was another resource I had spent too much of my first life pretending did not count.

I put the scrap away.

The yard chit went into the small inner fold of the shoulder bag where it would not fall out.

One copper still waited upstairs.

Fourteen copper still felt far.

The distance had changed shape again.

Not shorter.

More routes through it.

I liked that better.

# CHAPTER 324

## THE PRICE

Mara Quill charged two copper to tell you she did not know.

I respected that immediately.

I could not afford it.

I respected that less.

South Registry Row was not really a row. It was three crooked streets pretending they had agreed on a direction, all of them crowded with narrow shops whose signs assumed the reader already knew why they were there.

SEALS.

WEIGHTS.

OLD MARKS.

BONDS COPIED.

STONE RECORDS.

NO CLAIMS AFTER THIRD BELL.

That last one seemed less like a service and more like accumulated trauma.

I had left the fixed holdfast at home.

That had been deliberate.

The black Kiln yard chit stayed in the inner fold of my shoulder bag. The narrow scrap and wrapped charcoal stayed where they belonged. My one copper stayed upstairs.

I had come to learn what a question cost before carrying a two-copper object across half of Carrow to ask it.

This was progress.

In my first life I had once carried a cracked ward plate six miles to a man who charged me for opening the wrapping.

Then he charged me again for closing it.

I had been twenty-three and furious.

At fifty-nine I would have called that a cheap lesson.

The shop with Mara Quill's name was easy to miss because it did not have her name on it.

The sign said:

OLD HOUSINGS

MARKS READ

REGISTRY COPIES

NO BONDED WORK

Underneath, in smaller letters:

IF YOU WANT A PROMISE, BUY A PRIEST.

I stopped.

Then I went inside.

The room was long and shallow. One counter. Three stools. Shelves behind wire screens. A square window high on the back wall letting in enough light to make dust visible and nothing else attractive.

An old woman sat behind the counter with a lens strapped over one eye.

Not old-old.

Older than Lyssa. Younger than my first corpse.

Gray threaded through black hair pulled tight behind her head. Brown vest. White shirt. Ink on two fingers.

She was holding a brass hinge in wooden tongs.

I waited.

She turned it once.

Twice.

Set it down.

"No."

The man on the stool across from her said, "You didn't even open it."

"Correct."

"Then how do you know?"

"Know what?"

"That it isn't Rellan."

"I don't."

He stared at her.

She stared back.

"You said no."

"I said no to opening it."

"Why?"

"Because the pin is newer than the housing, the left leaf was filed after the stamp, and you told me it came sealed from your grandfather's wall. One of those things may be true. I do not need to open the hinge to know I dislike the story."

The man looked offended on behalf of his grandfather.

"He didn't lie."

"Then somebody lied to him."

"Can you tell me if it's Rellan?"

"Two copper for a mark read. Four if I have to expose the seat. More if you make me regret agreeing."

"Four?"

"Five now."

He stood.

"You're impossible."

"Frequently."

He took the hinge.

She added, "Do not sell it as sealed grandfather provenance."

"I know what I own."

"Then why did you come here?"

He left.

I moved aside for him.

He did not thank me.

Mara Quill lifted the lens from her eye.

"Next."

I looked behind me.

Nobody.

"Apparently me."

"Apparently."

I sat on the nearest stool.

She looked at my empty hands.

Then my bag.

Then my face.

"What did you leave at home?"

That was annoyingly good.

"A question."

"Those travel well."

"The object attached to it doesn't."

"Better. What kind?"

"Old fixed holdfast. Maybe."

Her expression did not change.

"Maybe fixed?"

"Fixed. Maybe holdfast."

"Who called it that?"

"Seller called it a holdfast."

"Seller called himself handsome too, I assume."

"He did not."

"Missed opportunity."

I liked her less than Jessa.

Possibly because she was winning.

"What do you charge?" I asked.

She pointed at a board on the wall beside me.

I had walked past it.

Excellent start.

MARK READ: 2 C

HOUSING READ: 3 C

OPEN SEAT: 4 C + MATERIALS

REGISTRY COPY: BY PAGE

PROVENANCE SEARCH: BY HOUR

FUNCTION CLAIM: NO

COMBAT CLAIM: NO

BONDED PIECE: NO

PURCHASE OFFER: SOMETIMES

I read the last line twice.

Mara watched me do it.

"That line causes trouble," she said.

"I imagine that's why you kept it."

"It saves longer trouble."

"Two copper just to read a mark?"

"If it takes less than ten minutes, yes."

"And if you don't know it?"

"Still two copper."

"That's excellent work."

"It took thirty years to make not knowing useful."

Fair.

I leaned one crutch against the stool.

"What does two copper buy me?"

"A description of what I can actually support from the visible mark. Maker if I know it. Shop if I know it. Period if the mark changed over time. Whether the stamp looks cut, struck, copied, recut, or married to a different housing. Sometimes what trade used that form. Sometimes nothing useful at all."

"No function."

"Not from a mark."

"No condition."

"Not from a mark."

"No value."

"Not from a mark."

"You have built an impressive business around disappointment."

"People pay more for confidence. They should pay more for limits."

That sounded like something Hessa would say if Hessa had discovered invoices.

I looked at the board again.

Two copper.

My holdfast had cost two.

That did not make the assessment overpriced.

It made the object cheap enough that assessing it could double my money committed before I learned anything.

Different problem.

"Do people bring you things worth less than the read?"

"Every week."

"Why?"

"Because they think worth is hiding inside the object and I can pull it out with a lens."

"Can you?"

"Sometimes."

"That seems dangerous to admit."

"You don't have two copper."

I looked at her.

"Rude."

"Accurate?"

"Also rude."

She waited.

I said, "I have one."

"Then don't bring me the object."

That answer came too quickly.

"You don't even know what it is."

"You have one copper. The object is at home. You came here first to ask what information costs. That means spending your only copper matters to you and you are not stupid enough to spend it on half a service."

"There isn't a one-copper service?"

"There is."

I looked at the board.

"Not listed."

"Questions."

"You charge for those?"

"Good ones."

"How much?"

"Depends whether you ask one."

I laughed.

She did not.

Maybe a little around the eyes.

"Fine," I said. "What can I learn before paying you?"

"Better question."

She reached under the counter and put a thin wooden card in front of me.

It had six boxes burned into it.

MARK

MATERIAL

MOVING PARTS

STONE OR CORE

VISIBLE DAMAGE

KNOWN USE

"Write those down before you come back," she said. "Draw the mark. Don't improve it. Don't clean it. Don't polish it. Don't oil it. Don't turn anything because you think movement will help you describe movement."

My face did something.

Her eyes narrowed.

"You turned something."

"At the shop. Once."

"What?"

"Ring."

"And?"

"Base held to the bench."

"For how long?"

"Long enough to demonstrate."

"How long?"

"Not measured."

"What surface?"

"Wooden bench."

"Load?"

"Seller pulled against it."

"How hard?"

"Hard enough to show it held. Not enough for me to call it a limit."

She nodded once.

"Good."

"That's free?"

"No. That was me deciding whether you're dangerous."

"Result?"

"Undecided."

Fair.

She tapped the wooden card.

"Bring description first if money is tight. I can sometimes tell you the question is not worth buying."

That surprised me.

"You turn away paid work?"

"I turn away stupid work. There is more paid work."

First-life me had known three assessors who would have had her murdered for saying that aloud.

One had eventually been murdered.

Unrelated.

Probably.

I looked at the last line on the board again.

PURCHASE OFFER: SOMETIMES.

"When do you buy?"

"When I want something."

"Very technical."

"You haven't paid for technical."

"Do you buy before assessment?"

"Sometimes."

"Isn't that a conflict?"

"Yes."

I waited.

She waited better.

"You just admit that?"

"If I want to buy, I tell the owner before I price anything. Then they can leave, hire someone else, or ask what I will pay."

"And if they ask what it's worth?"

"I tell them I am no longer the person to answer."

I sat back.

That was irritatingly clean.

"You know Rusk?" I asked.

"Which Rusk?"

"Guild cord. Cooper Street clearance yesterday. Old field brace. Four ribs. Red stone."

"That Rusk."

Nothing else.

"He gave me your name."

"Then he wanted you to stop asking him questions."

"Probably."

"Did it work?"

"Temporarily."

"Good enough."

I pulled the narrow scrap from my bag.

Not to hand it to her.

Just to check my own notes.

Mara saw the writing upside down.

"Fourteen?"

I covered it with my thumb.

"You read upside down."

"Costs extra right-side up."

"Brace sold for fourteen."

"And?"

"I thought that was a lot."

"It is."

"Not impossible."

"Most prices aren't."

"Some are."

"Then they are not prices for you."

That landed harder than it deserved.

I had spent too much of my first life around people who treated money as proof of rank. Gold meant you had arrived. Silver meant you were climbing. Copper meant you were counting meals.

Then I had become S-class and discovered there were still doors with prices I could not casually pay.

Better doors.

More expensive mistakes.

Same arithmetic.

"I want to be able to move when something like that appears again," I said.

Mara's expression changed for the first time.

Not warmer.

More attentive.

"Then don't start by buying assessments."

I blinked.

"You are terrible at sales."

"You don't need sales. You need capital."

There it was.

Ugly word.

Useful word.

"How much?"

"For what?"

"Enough."

"Enough is not a number."

"Fourteen was."

"Yesterday."

"Six opened it."

"Yesterday."

"Eleven was serious trade money."

"Yesterday."

I frowned.

She tapped the counter.

"If you decide you need fourteen because one brace sold for fourteen, you will spend six months becoming ready for yesterday."

That was annoying.

Also correct.

"Then what do I become ready for?"

"Choice."

I hated answers like that.

She continued before I could complain.

"One copper lets you choose among one-copper things. Five lets you choose among some five-copper things and walk away from bad ones. Twenty does not mean you buy a twenty-copper thing. It means you can still have money after buying eight."

That was better.

Not profound.

Just structurally useful.

Reserve was not a target price.

It was room around a decision.

I looked down at the wooden card.

MARK.

MATERIAL.

MOVING PARTS.

STONE OR CORE.

VISIBLE DAMAGE.

KNOWN USE.

"Can I keep this?"

"One bit."

I stared at her.

She stared back.

Then she smiled.

Barely.

"Take it."

"Cruel."

"You have no bits."

"How do you know that?"

"You told me you had one copper with the expression of a man who would have mentioned smaller money if it existed."

I put the card in my bag.

"I dislike you."

"Two copper to confirm."

I stood.

My right hand settled onto the crutch grip.

"One more question."

"You haven't asked a paid one yet."

"What makes a question worth paying for?"

She looked at me for a long second.

Then she pointed toward the door.

"When the answer changes what you do."

I stopped.

That one was free too.

Probably because it was dangerous.

Outside, Registry Row had become busier. A courier pushed past carrying three sealed tubes. A woman argued with a weights clerk about whether a chipped brass standard could still be copied. Somewhere farther down the crooked street, a bell rang twice.

I moved into the flow.

The holdfast was still upstairs.

Untested.

Unassessed.

Still mine.

My one copper was still upstairs too.

Also mine.

Nothing had increased.

That was not the same as nothing changing.

At the next corner I stopped, took out the narrow scrap, and wrote beneath yesterday's Kiln notes:

MARA QUILL

MARK READ 2 C

HOUSING 3 C

OPEN 4 C + MAT

QUESTIONS FIRST

Then, after a moment:

DON'T SAVE FOR YESTERDAY

I looked at that.

Too dramatic.

I rubbed it out with my thumb until it became a gray smear.

Then I wrote:

RESERVE = CHOICE AFTER PRICE

Better.

Still annoying.

I put the scrap away.

Fourteen copper had looked like a wall yesterday.

Today it looked more like one door in a street full of doors.

Some cost two.

Some cost fourteen.

Some cost enough that nobody bothered painting the number where people like me could see it.

Fine.

I did not need every door.

I needed to stop arriving with exactly enough for none of them.

# CHAPTER 325

## THE NIGHT LINE

The job paid two copper because nobody wanted to stand in the square after dark and tell strangers where not to stand.

I understood immediately.

That was exactly the kind of work strangers made difficult.

The notice was nailed to the side of a public board near the lower market, under three missing-cat notices and one offer to sharpen six knives for the price of five if all six belonged to the same person.

NIGHT LINE HANDS WANTED.

THIRD BELL TO LATE CHIME.

WEST GLASS SQUARE.

TWO COPPER.

KEEP PUBLIC OUTSIDE MARKED LINE.

NO LIFTING REQUIRED.

REPORT TO SEL VARRIN.

I read it twice.

Then a third time because I had learned recently that prices improved when I actually read the rest of the words attached to them.

Two copper.

No lifting.

Night.

Crowd work.

Marked line.

That sounded less like labor and more like being blamed by people who wanted to stand six inches closer to something dangerous.

I had done worse for free.

A second notice beneath it offered one bit for unloading sacks before sunset.

Closer.

Shorter.

Probably easier.

I stood between them long enough that a woman beside me said, "You taking the sacks?"

"No."

"Good."

She tore the sack notice from the board.

Apparently my economic hesitation had competition.

I took the night notice down.

Not because two copper solved anything.

It did not.

One copper upstairs plus two earned would make three.

Three was not fourteen.

Three was also not one.

More importantly, it was the first time since Mara's shop that I had looked at ordinary work and asked not only whether I could do it, but what it did to the space around my next decision.

That sounded pretentious.

So I stopped thinking it.

West Glass Square sat farther north than I usually wandered without a reason. I had passed the edge once with Lyssa months ago, but never crossed the center.

The name came from six tall windows set into the guildhall on the west side, all made from old green-tinted glass that turned the late light strange.

By third bell the square was already half closed.

Chalk marks made a wide rectangle around the center paving. Short poles stood at each corner. A thin cord ran between them at knee height.

Inside the rectangle, four workers were assembling something that looked like a chandelier designed by a person who hated ceilings.

A bronze central mast rose from a three-legged base. Six curved arms extended outward. Each arm ended in a shallow glass bowl the size of a wash basin.

The bowls were empty.

For now.

A man with a red scarf stood near a folding table checking names against a paper.

"Night line?" he asked when I approached.

I held up the notice.

"Unless I misunderstood the concept dramatically."

He looked at my crutches.

Then the notice.

Then me.

"No lifting."

"I noticed."

"Can you stand until late chime?"

"With breaks."

"Can you walk the line?"

"Yes."

"Can you shout?"

"Professionally."

He almost smiled.

"Sel Varrin."

"Greg."

He made a mark on the paper.

"North side. First hour. Rotate west after fourth bell. Sit if you need to, but keep eyes up. If anyone crosses the cord, put them back outside. Don't touch the mast. Don't touch the bowls. Don't touch anything the glassworkers carry."

"What if something catches fire?"

"Tell me."

"What if you're on fire?"

"Tell someone else."

Reasonable.

I looked toward the bronze structure.

"What is it?"

"Public light trial."

"Whose?"

"Not your problem."

Even better.

I liked jobs with boundaries.

A woman at the table handed me a flat strip of blue cloth.

"Tie that where people can see it."

I tied it around the strap of my shoulder bag.

She looked at it.

"Good enough."

The other line hands were already taking positions.

A thick man with a shaved head had the south side. Two younger women split east and west. I took north.

The cord was not magical.

I checked because it would have been embarrassing to spend the entire evening respecting a string for mystical reasons when ordinary rope was sufficient.

The first hour was easy.

Children tried to duck under it.

Adults pretended not to see it.

One old man stepped directly over the cord, looked at the bronze mast, and said, "I was here before the line."

"The line disagrees."

"I stood there yesterday."

"Congratulations."

"You can't tell me where to stand."

"I am being paid specifically to do that."

He stared at me.

Then at the blue cloth.

"By who?"

I pointed at Sel.

"Man with paper."

The old man looked at Sel.

Sel looked back.

The old man stepped outside the cord.

Two copper was already earning itself.

Near fourth bell, the glassworkers brought out the bowls.

Not the empty ones.

Six new bowls came from padded crates.

Each was clear except for a cloudy knot in the center, like someone had trapped a thumbprint inside the glass.

They seated one bowl onto each bronze arm.

No one applauded.

Good crowd.

A woman inside the line walked the full circle checking every bowl twice.

She wore thick leather sleeves and gray lenses over her eyes.

Sel moved toward her.

They spoke quietly.

Then he came to the line hands.

"When the trial starts, nobody crosses. Not even if they dropped something inside. Not even if they know someone. Not even if they say the city owes them money."

The shaved-head man asked, "Has that happened?"

"Yes."

"Which one?"

"All of them."

I respected cities.

Sel continued.

"If a bowl goes dark, shout dark and point. If one goes blue, shout blue and point. If one cracks, get people away from that side."

One of the women on east said, "How far?"

"To the paving seam."

There was a second seam about twelve feet beyond the cord.

Useful.

"If the mast drops?" I asked.

Sel looked at me.

"Run."

"Alternative?"

He glanced at my crutches.

"Move away urgently."

"Better."

The gray-lensed woman heard us and laughed.

Then the trial began.

No chant.

No dramatic countdown.

One worker at the base turned a brass key.

The cloudy knots inside all six bowls brightened.

White first.

Then pale gold.

The entire square changed.

Not brighter exactly.

Cleaner.

Shadows pulled inward. The green guildhall windows stopped throwing color across the paving. Faces looked sharper from farther away. Every line between stone blocks became suddenly obvious.

I had seen public light systems before.

Not this one.

Old Greg had slept under ward lamps, camp lamps, battle lamps, healer lamps, tunnel lamps, and one memorable lamp that attracted every biting insect within half a mile.

This was different mostly because I was standing still enough to notice it.

The crowd noticed too.

People pressed toward the cord.

There it was.

The actual job.

"Outside the line," I said.

A boy leaned over.

"But I can see better."

"You can see from there."

"Not the bottom."

"Then imagine the bottom."

His mother pulled him back by the collar.

The north crowd thickened faster than the other sides because the street behind me fed directly from market row.

I shifted along the cord.

Three people back.

One basket farther out.

A man with a cane tried to hook the cord down with it.

I put my crutch tip on the cord before he could.

"No."

"I wasn't crossing."

"You were improving the line."

"It blocks the view."

"That is one of its stronger qualities."

He gave me a look and moved left.

The light intensified.

The bowls did not glow much themselves. The air beneath each one did.

Six pale columns formed around the central mast, not beams exactly, more like clear places in the evening.

People became quieter.

That lasted almost twenty seconds.

Then someone on the west side shouted, "BLUE!"

Every head turned.

One bowl had changed.

Not fully blue.

The cloudy knot at its center had gone cobalt.

Sel pointed.

"West back to seam."

The west line hand started moving people.

The problem was everyone else wanted to move west too.

Of course they did.

The interesting thing had happened there.

My north crowd surged sideways along the cord.

A woman bumped my right crutch.

I caught myself.

"Back."

Nobody listened.

I had spent enough time backstage to know a crowd did not hear instructions when it thought the real event was somewhere else.

So I stopped telling them where not to go.

I pointed hard toward the east side of the mast.

"You can see the color change better from that angle. East side. Keep outside the seam."

Half the people nearest me turned the other direction.

Not because I knew that was true.

It was probably true enough.

More importantly, it split the flow.

The pressure on the north-west corner eased.

Sel saw it.

He did not praise me.

Excellent.

He just pointed two fingers east and repeated louder, "Better view east. Keep moving."

Now it became official.

People moved.

The west bowl stayed blue for maybe ten heartbeats.

Then returned to gold.

The gray-lensed woman checked something at the base.

Nobody died.

Strong trial so far.

At fourth bell we rotated.

I took west.

My hands were starting to ache.

I sat on a low stone post just outside the seam for a few minutes, keeping the cord in view.

A little girl stared at my left trouser leg.

Then at the crutches.

Then at the light.

"Would it grow back in that?"

Her father went rigid.

I looked at the glowing bowls.

"Probably not."

"Why?"

"Wrong kind of light."

"What kind grows legs?"

"Expensive."

Her father made a noise that might have been a cough.

She accepted this and returned to watching the mast.

I rested another minute.

Then stood.

The second hour was less crowded and more dangerous because people had decided they understood the rules.

That was always worse.

One man stepped over the cord while looking directly at me.

"I work glass."

"Not inside this line tonight."

"I know what they're doing."

"Then you know where the line is."

He stepped back.

Another woman tried to hand a wrapped parcel across to one of the workers.

"For Eren."

"After trial."

"It's his supper."

"Then he'll be hungry safely."

She looked offended.

I sympathized with Eren.

The bowls cycled three more times.

Gold.

Dim.

Gold again.

No blue.

Then the south bowl cracked.

The sound was tiny.

A wineglass sound.

Almost nothing.

The shaved-head line hand shouted before I located it.

"CRACK SOUTH!"

Good lungs.

Sel was already moving.

"South to seam. East corner clear. West hold."

The south crowd backed up badly.

People turned instead of stepping straight back.

Someone dropped a basket.

Apples rolled under the cord.

A child went after them.

Of course.

I was twenty feet away.

The nearest east line woman grabbed the child's coat before he crossed.

The bowl made another tiny sound.

A pale line appeared across the glass.

The light beneath it bent sideways.

Not a beam.

A distortion.

Everything behind it looked half an inch misplaced.

Sel shouted, "Paving seam. Now."

This time everyone listened.

The gray-lensed woman did not run toward the bowl.

She went to the base.

Good.

One worker turned the brass key.

Nothing happened.

The south bowl stayed lit.

Second turn.

Still lit.

The crowd made one collective noise.

Not panic yet.

Considering panic.

I knew that sound too.

The west side started drifting backward even though our bowl was fine.

That was acceptable.

Then two men behind me turned and pushed into people trying to leave north.

Bad geometry.

I pointed toward the west alley.

"West alley open. Use it. Don't cross north flow."

The first man ignored me.

The second followed my hand.

Then others did.

The flow split.

Again.

Stage blocking with worse actors.

The cracked bowl flickered.

The distortion jumped.

The gray-lensed woman pulled a red handle at the base.

All six bowls went dark at once.

The square vanished.

Not literally.

But after that much clean light, ordinary evening felt like someone had thrown cloth over my head.

People shouted.

I planted both crutches.

"Stay where you are. Eyes adjust."

That instruction worked because nobody could see enough to improvise.

For once darkness improved public behavior.

The guildhall windows slowly returned as green rectangles.

Street lamps became visible.

Faces reappeared.

The south bowl stayed intact.

Cracked, but intact.

The gray-lensed woman said something to Sel.

He nodded.

Then raised both hands.

"Trial over. Clear the square."

Someone booed.

Of course.

A magical light fixture had nearly failed in public and somebody wanted an encore.

I admired consistency.

Clearing the square took longer than the emergency.

People wanted explanations.

Sel gave none.

People wanted to know whether tomorrow's trial would still happen.

Sel said he did not know.

People wanted refunds.

There had been no admission fee.

A man demanded one anyway.

Eventually the square emptied.

The line hands gathered near the folding table.

My hands hurt enough that opening and closing my fingers felt useful.

The shaved-head man said, "You do this often?"

"Stand near things that go wrong?"

"Crowds."

"Theatre."

He nodded like that explained everything.

It did not.

Maybe enough.

Sel counted from a small lockbox.

Two copper each.

Actual copper.

He put mine on the table.

I looked at them.

Then picked them up.

No ceremony.

No moral lesson.

No sudden feeling that I had become financially responsible.

They were money.

That was useful enough.

Sel said, "You split the north surge well."

"I lied about the east view."

"Was it worse?"

"I don't know."

"Then you redirected."

"That is a generous verb."

"Want tomorrow if they run again?"

There it was.

Easy answer would have been yes.

Two copper again.

Three total would become five.

Reserve.

Choice.

Doors.

I looked at the cracked south bowl being lowered into a padded crate.

"Are they running again?"

"Don't know."

"Then ask me when you know."

Sel nodded.

No promise.

Good.

I put the two copper in the inner fold of my shoulder bag, separate from the black Kiln chit.

The bag suddenly felt more important than it had yesterday.

Not heavier.

Just more worth paying attention to.

On the walk home, I passed the public board again.

The sack notice was gone.

The knife-sharpening offer remained.

One new notice had appeared.

MORNING CART COUNT.

ONE BIT.

I read it.

Then kept walking.

Not because one bit was beneath me.

It was still money.

But tomorrow morning had other value too.

Sleep.

My hands.

The possibility that Sel might call if the trial ran again.

The possibility that something better might appear.

That was the part I had not understood when Mara said choice.

Reserve was not only the coins after a purchase.

It was the ability to say no before one.

At home, I went upstairs before anyone could ask why I smelled like square dust and public disappointment.

My original copper sat where I had left it.

I placed the two new ones beside it.

Three.

I looked at them for a while.

Not reverently.

Counting was allowed.

Three copper.

Zero bits.

Still nowhere near the brace.

Closer to a housing read.

Closer to a mark read without emptying myself.

Closer to buying something ordinary and still having money afterward.

Closer was dangerous because it encouraged arithmetic.

I took out the narrow scrap.

Under Mara's notes I wrote:

NIGHT LINE 2 C

WEST GLASS

CROWD MOVES TOWARD INTEREST

SPLIT FLOW > PUSH BACK

Then I stopped.

The last two lines looked like I was trying to turn one evening into doctrine.

I rubbed them partly out.

Better.

I wrote only:

3 C TOTAL

Then below it:

DON'T TAKE EVERY COIN JUST BECAUSE IT'S THERE

I stared at that.

Too much like advice.

I hated advice written by myself most of all.

I rubbed that out too.

The gray smear joined yesterday's gray smear.

My record was becoming more honest through abrasion.

I put the scrap away.

The two new copper stayed beside the old one.

Three was not enough.

Three was enough to make the next question different.

# CHAPTER 326

## THE LOT

Three copper bought me the right to make a bad decision with confidence.

This was apparently progress.

The morning after West Glass, my shoulders felt as though someone had spent the night tightening them with a small wrench.

Not injured.

Just used.

There was a difference, and at nineteen I was finally old enough to appreciate it while still being young enough to complain.

I sat at the table with one crutch against my chair and rolled my right shoulder until something clicked.

Lyssa looked up from a strip of dark cloth.

"Good click?"

"Probably."

"Excellent medical system."

"I've survived worse."

"You say that about everything."

"It keeps being true."

She went back to the cloth.

I had not told her about the three copper yet.

Not because it was secret.

Because announcing money made it feel like money was about to leave.

This was irrational.

I had been rich enough in my first life to stop counting ordinary meals and still developed the habit of checking whether my purse existed every time I stood up.

Money changed.

Paranoia diversified.

Tavi came through the room carrying a wooden spoon like a sword.

"You working today?"

"Not yet."

"Then you're not working."

"That is a brutal interpretation of time."

He stabbed the air once and left.

Lyssa said, "He learned it from you."

"Impossible. I use more words."

I ate.

Then I checked the public board.

Not because I had decided to work.

Because three copper was enough to make the board interesting in a different way.

Yesterday I had looked for what paid best among things I could reasonably do.

Today I looked for what the money might let me do next.

There were two hauling notices, one copy job requiring clean script, a request for somebody who knew how to remove a goat from a tiled roof, and a card advertising six jars of preserved pears at a price that suggested the pears had political influence.

No Sel notice.

No West Glass trial.

Good.

Or bad.

Mostly not my problem.

I kept walking.

The lower market was already crowded. A fish seller was arguing with a customer over whether a fish with one eye cost less because it had seen less ocean. A woman had three copper kettles stacked on her head while carrying nothing in either hand, which seemed like showing off.

I passed the regular tool stalls.

Then the broken-tool stalls.

Then the stalls that called themselves old-tool stalls because broken sounded less profitable.

I was not hunting artifacts.

That sentence became less true the farther I walked.

Not because I expected to find one.

Meaningful old pieces did not sit in every basket waiting for a reincarnated idiot to recognize them.

Mostly baskets contained bent hinges, cracked lamp housings, worn kitchen stones, dead seals, obsolete fittings, and objects whose only hidden property was tetanus.

Still.

I had three copper.

Three copper was not much.

Three copper was enough that looking stopped being completely theoretical.

That mattered.

A stall near the end of Tool Lane had no sign.

Just a canvas roof, a narrow table, and an old man with both hands wrapped around a cup.

The table held six lots separated by chalk lines.

Not six objects.

Lots.

A box of brass fasteners.

Three cracked lamp cups.

A bundle of thin iron rods.

A tray of mixed stone fittings.

A small wooden case with no lid.

And a shallow basket containing what looked like the contents of a repairer's bad month.

I slowed.

The old man said, "Basket is one copper."

I had not asked.

"Good morning to you too."

"Morning is free. Basket is one copper."

"Why?"

"Because half copper doesn't exist in my patience."

I looked at the basket.

"What's in it?"

"Things."

"Useful."

"Somebody thought so once."

There were perhaps twenty pieces inside.

Two buckles.

A blackened hinge.

Four stone buttons.

A broken ring with three holes around its edge.

A flat copper plate bent at one corner.

Something that might have been a lock tongue.

Two pieces of cloudy glass.

A small iron hook.

A pale ceramic cylinder the length of my thumb.

And beneath them, partly hidden by a strip of leather, a dark oval no larger than a plum pit.

I stopped looking at it.

Not dramatically.

Just moved my eyes.

The old man drank from his cup.

I looked at the brass-fastener box instead.

"How much?"

"Two."

"The basket has more."

"Basket has worse."

Reasonable market.

I took Mara's wooden checklist card from my bag.

The old man noticed.

"You buying or praying?"

"Trying not to buy garbage."

"Then don't buy anything."

Excellent seller.

I crouched as far as my balance allowed, then decided dignity was cheaper than falling and pulled over an empty crate with my right foot.

"Can I sit?"

"If you don't break it."

I sat.

The basket stayed on the table.

I did not touch it.

MARK.

MATERIAL.

MOVING PARTS.

STONE OR CORE.

VISIBLE DAMAGE.

KNOWN USE.

The dark oval had no visible mark from this angle.

Material was harder.

Not stone.

Maybe fired glass.

Maybe old resin.

Maybe horn polished until the grain disappeared.

No moving parts visible.

No obvious core.

Damage unknown.

Known use absolutely none.

Excellent.

Mara would have been proud of how little I knew.

The reason I had stopped was not the oval itself.

It was the leather strip lying over it.

The strip had a burned line down its center and three tiny holes at one end.

Old mounting strap.

Maybe.

And the oval had a shallow groove around its edge.

Not enough to identify it.

Enough to remind me of something.

First life.

A road north of Teren Ford.

Rain.

A pack frame with one strap torn through.

A woman named Sera swearing because her left boot had filled with water.

Not useful.

Then later.

Same trip.

A night shelter with six wet people and a little black disk hanging from a nail beside the door.

Someone had touched it before sleeping.

Or after waking.

No.

That memory was wrong.

Maybe different trip.

I hated partial memories because they arrived with the confidence of complete ones.

I looked at the basket again.

"Where did this lot come from?"

"Repair sweep."

"Whose?"

"Mine now."

"Before yours."

"South warehouse clearance."

"Which warehouse?"

"The one that closed."

I waited.

He drank.

I was not going to win this through silence.

"Trade?"

"Mixed."

"How mixed?"

"Door fittings. Harness. Lamp work. Cart pieces. Two boxes marked household. One marked shrine and full of hinges."

"This basket from one box?"

"No."

That reduced provenance almost to weather.

Good to know.

"Anything in it work?"

"The buckle probably."

"Magically."

He looked at me for the first time with actual attention.

Then at the checklist card.

"If I knew, basket wouldn't be one copper."

There it was.

Rational seller.

Not stupid.

Not secretly blind.

He did not know because the lot was mixed low-value repair sweep and testing every piece cost more than dumping it.

That did not mean anything magical was inside.

It meant information had a price too.

I leaned closer without touching.

The dark oval caught light along one edge.

A thin pale line appeared in the groove.

Then vanished when a cloud moved.

Glass, maybe.

No.

Not enough.

"Can I turn the basket?"

"Basket, yes. Pieces, no."

I rotated the whole shallow basket a quarter turn.

The oval shifted slightly against the leather.

Its underside became visible.

There was a mark.

Barely.

Not a maker stamp.

Three short cuts forming an open triangle.

My stomach tightened.

Not because I knew it.

Because I knew the family of marks.

Maybe.

Road equipment.

Old field convenience pieces.

Things designed to be used by people too tired to read instructions.

Or I was inventing a pattern because I wanted the basket to matter.

Both were possible.

I took out charcoal.

"Can I draw the mark?"

"Draw whatever you like."

I copied the three cuts onto the narrow scrap.

Not improved.

Mara's rule.

The left cut was shorter.

The lower one might have been wear rather than intentional.

I wrote that too.

The old man watched.

"One copper," he reminded me.

"You said."

"You are making a copper face."

"What does that look like?"

"Like you're trying to make one copper become information."

Annoyingly precise.

I had three.

Buying the basket would leave two.

That was different from buying Mara's housing read and leaving zero.

Choice after price.

I could spend one and still have two.

That did not make the basket good.

It made the decision possible.

I inspected the rest.

The copper plate had a stamped number, probably inventory.

One stone button had a hairline crack.

The ceramic cylinder was hollow and smelled faintly of lamp oil.

The broken ring was ordinary iron.

One cloudy glass piece had a silver thread inside it, but the thread ended at the fracture. Could have been decorative. Could have been dead channel work. Could have been nothing.

The black oval remained the only piece that pulled at memory.

Not enough.

I stood.

"Half copper."

The old man lifted his cup.

"No."

"One copper and you keep the buckles."

"No."

"One copper and I get the basket too."

"You already get the basket."

"Actual basket?"

"Yes."

I looked at the shallow woven basket.

That improved the deal by an amount too embarrassing to calculate.

"Why not separate the pieces?"

"Because then I would have to sell twenty pieces."

There was the actual discount.

Labor.

Attention.

Table space.

He was selling the problem cheaply because sorting it was not his business today.

I reached into my bag.

Stopped.

"Anything dangerous you know about?"

The old man lowered his cup.

"Known dangerous? No."

"Unknown dangerous?"

"Everything is unknown dangerous if you work hard enough."

"Any piece from a death?"

"Not that I was told."

"Fire?"

"Warehouse had one old scorch wall. These lots weren't marked from it."

"Bonded?"

"Nothing sold to me as bonded."

"Restricted?"

"Not sold to me as restricted."

Careful wording.

Good.

"Returns?"

"No."

Of course.

I paid one copper.

The coin left my hand without pain.

That was new.

Not because one copper had become nothing.

Because I still had two.

The old man pushed the basket toward me.

"Congratulations."

"On what?"

"Owning my problem."

Fair.

I did not put the oval in my pocket.

I did not touch it at all.

I carried the basket level against my right hip with one forearm while using the crutch awkwardly on that side.

This lasted six steps.

Then I stopped.

Terrible plan.

I moved the shoulder bag across my body, tied the basket handle to the bag strap with the leather strip from inside the lot, tested the hang, hated it, untied it, and finally paid a nearby fruit seller one bit I did not possess in exchange for nothing because I did not possess a bit.

That plan had a flaw.

The fruit seller stared at me.

"You all right?"

"Financially inconsistent."

She pointed at a stack of old wrapping cloth.

"Take one."

"Free?"

"You bought nothing."

"That usually costs less."

"Take the cloth before I change my mind."

I took the cloth.

No money changed hands.

I wrapped the basket and tied it to the top of my shoulder bag tightly enough that it stopped swinging.

Better.

Still stupid-looking.

Functional won.

At home, Lyssa saw the basket before I got through the door.

"No."

"You don't know what it is."

"Neither do you."

"That's not the point."

"That is exactly the point."

Tavi appeared behind her.

"Treasure?"

"Repair garbage," Lyssa said.

"Potential repair garbage," I corrected.

Tavi reached.

I lifted the basket.

"No touching."

His hand stopped.

That was progress too.

"Why?"

"Because I don't know what some of it does."

"Then why did you buy it?"

Lyssa looked at me.

I looked at Tavi.

"I dislike this household."

"How much?" Lyssa asked.

"One copper."

She stared.

Not horrified.

Just recalculating me.

"For garbage."

"For the basket."

"Greg."

"And possible old field hardware."

"There it is."

I carried the lot upstairs.

The holdfast remained on the high shelf.

I cleared a patch of floor beneath the window, laid down one of my older scraps of sailcloth, and set the basket in the center.

Tavi stayed at the doorway because I told him to.

Lyssa leaned against the frame behind him.

"Are we exploding?"

"Not intentionally."

"Comforting."

I took Mara's checklist card out.

Then, one at a time, I moved the obviously mundane pieces out of the basket using a folded cloth around my fingers.

Not because cloth made unknown magic safe.

Because grime existed.

Buckles.

Hinge.

Buttons.

Copper plate.

Lock tongue.

Iron hook.

Ceramic lamp piece.

Broken ring.

Cloudy glass.

I did not activate anything.

I did not turn the oval.

I did not press the mark.

I did not scrape it clean.

I simply exposed it fully.

Dark oval.

About two inches long.

One inch wide.

Groove around edge.

Three-cut open triangle on underside.

One end had a tiny hole through it.

Not a stone.

Not ordinary glass either.

I could see faint depth under the surface, like smoke trapped under ice.

Tavi whispered, "Treasure."

"Still unknown."

Lyssa said, "You paid one copper for unknown."

"And nineteen pieces of garbage."

"Better."

I counted.

Eighteen.

"Eighteen pieces of garbage."

"Excellent investment."

I smiled despite myself.

Then the oval moved.

Not much.

A twitch.

I froze.

Tavi stepped backward without being told.

Good child.

Lyssa straightened.

The oval moved again.

One end rotated perhaps half an inch across the sailcloth.

Then stopped.

I had not touched it.

Nobody had.

The window was open.

Air moved through the room.

The sailcloth shifted slightly.

Possible explanation.

I closed the window.

Waited.

Nothing.

Good.

I opened it again.

Lyssa said, "That feels like testing."

"Environmental observation."

"That sounds like testing with extra syllables."

Fair.

I left the window open.

A breeze moved the curtain.

The sailcloth edge lifted.

The oval stayed still.

Then, when the breeze stopped, it rotated another fraction.

Wrong direction for the cloth.

I stared.

No glow.

No sound.

No mana sensation I trusted.

Just movement.

Small.

Slow.

The pointed end, if it had a pointed end, was now aimed roughly toward the doorway.

Tavi moved left.

The oval did not follow him.

Good.

Lyssa moved right.

Nothing.

I shifted my crutch.

Nothing.

Then somewhere downstairs the front door opened.

The oval turned.

Not toward the door.

Away from it.

A quarter inch.

Then stopped.

I felt the old memory catch.

Wet road.

Night shelter.

Black disk beside the door.

Someone touching it before sleep.

No.

Someone hanging it where it could move.

And in the morning it had pointed toward...

I could not get the rest.

Not yet.

"Do you know?" Lyssa asked.

"No."

That answer felt clean.

"Do you think you know?"

"Worse."

"Good."

I looked at Mara's checklist.

KNOWN USE.

Blank.

I wrote:

MOVES WITHOUT TOUCH

Then beneath it:

TWICE? THREE TIMES

Then:

DOOR OPENED -> TURNED AWAY? ONE OBSERVATION

I underlined the question mark, not the claim.

Hessa would have approved.

Probably while making me remove the word `away` until I established an angle.

I added:

NO ACTIVATION BY ME

NO MANA ATTEMPT

Lyssa read over my shoulder.

"You bought a thing that moves."

"Maybe."

"It moved."

"The question is why."

"You are becoming Mara."

"Cruel."

"Two copper to confirm."

I looked at her.

She smiled.

Apparently I had made the mistake of bringing jokes home.

I wrapped the oval separately in clean cloth.

Not one of the three unused gray household sheets.

I was not sacrificing good cloth to a mystery plum pit.

I put it in the shallow wooden case from the lot, because the case fit badly but adequately, then set the case on the floor beside the high shelf rather than on it.

Then reconsidered Tavi.

High shelf.

Different side from the holdfast.

No contact between them.

The remaining eighteen pieces stayed in the basket on the floor until I could decide whether any were worth keeping.

I counted my money.

Two copper.

Zero bits.

One copper gone.

A month ago I might have felt the loss first.

Today I felt the difference between buying a one-copper portrait and buying a one-copper basket of uncertain hardware.

Not because art was foolish.

Because I wanted this question more.

That was what money was for when it stopped being only survival.

Not virtue.

Preference.

I took out the narrow scrap.

Under `RESERVE = CHOICE AFTER PRICE`, I wrote:

TOOL LANE LOT 1 C

DARK OVAL / 3-CUT OPEN TRIANGLE

MOVES WITHOUT TOUCH

NO CLAIM YET

Then I added the thing that mattered most:

2 C LEFT

I almost crossed it out.

Too much purse counting.

Then left it.

This time the number was not fear.

It was runway.

On the shelf, the wrapped oval did nothing.

For nearly an hour.

Then Cala came home.

The front door closed downstairs.

A moment later, from inside the little wooden case, something made one soft click.

I looked up.

The holdfast did not move.

The case did not move.

Nothing glowed.

Nothing exploded.

One click.

That was all.

I smiled.

Not because I knew what I had bought.

Because for one copper, I had finally bought something worth finding out.

# CHAPTER 327

## THE LAST DOOR

The thing clicked every time I went through a door.

Not every door.

That would have been useful.

It clicked often enough to be suspicious and irregularly enough to make me hate it.

The first click came when I left the apartment.

I had put the dark oval in my shoulder bag because leaving it upstairs after buying it felt like admitting I had purchased decorative uncertainty.

I had not activated it.

I had not pressed the mark.

I had not threaded anything through the tiny hole.

I had wrapped it in the same clean cloth, placed it in the shallow wooden case, and tucked the case upright in the outer pocket of my bag where it could not touch the holdfast because the holdfast remained upstairs.

Separate problems.

Important principle.

I stepped through the front door.

Click.

Soft.

From the bag.

I stopped on the landing.

Lyssa, behind me, almost walked into my back.

"What?"

"It clicked."

"You click."

"Different click."

"Useful distinction."

I opened the bag.

The case had not opened.

The oval had not escaped.

Nothing glowed.

Nothing smelled like burning hair.

Good start.

I closed the bag.

Went back inside.

No click.

Stepped out again.

Nothing.

Lyssa folded her arms.

"Strong science."

"It did it once."

"So did Tavi yesterday with a spoon."

"He does that constantly."

"More reliable artifact."

I went down the stairs.

The building door opened.

I crossed onto the street.

Click.

I stopped again.

Lyssa was no longer behind me.

Good.

I turned around, went back through the building door, crossed the threshold, waited.

Nothing.

Out again.

Nothing.

"Excellent," I muttered.

A woman passing with a basket looked at me and decided not to ask.

Carrow had manners when it mattered.

I wrote on the narrow scrap:

FRONT DOOR OUT -> CLICK

BUILDING DOOR OUT -> CLICK

REPEAT SAME DOOR -> NO CLICK

Then I stared at that.

Too early.

I added:

SO FAR

Hessa would have approved of the insult.

I was supposed to be taking a receipt to Cala's dye man.

Not her dye man in the romantic sense.

Carrow was a difficult city to describe concisely.

A supplier two streets south of the old cooper row had sent the wrong shade cord with a previous bundle. Cala had already handled the actual correction. My job was to carry a folded receipt to a back counter because I was walking that direction anyway.

Small errand.

No money.

No mystery.

Perfect conditions for a mystery to become irritating.

I crossed into the narrow dye shop.

Click.

This time I heard it clearly.

I stopped halfway through the doorway.

The clerk behind the front counter said, "You coming in?"

"Apparently."

"That's usually how doors work."

I handed over the receipt.

"Back counter," he said.

"Cala's correction."

"Back counter."

I looked toward a narrow hallway beside hanging blue cloth.

"How far back?"

"Until someone looks annoyed."

Excellent directions.

I went through the hall curtain.

No click.

Through a wooden door.

Click.

Then down three steps into a workroom smelling strongly of wet fiber and vinegar.

A woman at a table looked up.

Not annoyed.

Wrong person.

"Receipt?" I asked.

She pointed farther back.

"Tally room."

Another door.

Click.

I stopped.

She watched me.

"You all right?"

"My bag has opinions."

"Leave it outside if it starts talking."

Reasonable policy.

The tally room contained one man, four shelves, three ledgers, and enough bundled cord to strangle a small army.

He took the receipt.

Read it.

Stamped it once.

"Done."

I waited.

"That's all?"

"Did you want an argument?"

"No."

"Then done."

I turned to leave.

The dark oval clicked before I reached the door.

Not crossing it.

Before.

I froze.

The tally man looked up.

"Now what?"

I opened my bag.

The shallow case had shifted.

Not much.

The oval inside was pressed against one side of the cloth wrapping.

I set the bag on an empty stool and opened the case without touching the oval directly.

The oval had rotated within the cloth.

Its narrow end pointed toward the door I had just used.

Maybe.

That was the first time the shape looked directional enough to call one end narrow.

I moved around the stool.

The oval did not follow me.

Good.

I turned the case ninety degrees.

The oval stayed where it was relative to the room.

Not the case.

My skin prickled.

The tally man leaned over.

"What is that?"

"Unknown."

"You carry unknown things into dye shops?"

"Only the small ones."

He stepped back.

Smart man.

I lifted the whole case and carried it three feet left.

The oval rotated slowly.

Still toward the door.

I stopped.

There it was.

Not proof of what the door meant.

But orientation.

Toward a doorway I had crossed.

Maybe the last one.

Maybe a particular one.

Maybe a material seam.

Maybe the receipt.

Maybe the tally man was secretly magnetic.

I looked at him.

He looked offended.

Probably not magnetic.

I covered the oval again.

"Done?" he asked.
