"For now."

"Good."

I went out through the tally-room door.

Click.

I stopped immediately and reopened the case on a barrel top.

The oval had rotated.

Now it pointed back through the tally-room door.

I felt the first-life memory catch hard enough to hurt.

Wet boots.

Road shelter.

Six people asleep.

A black piece hanging from a nail beside the door.

One of the younger scouts asking why it mattered.

An older woman saying, "Because dark makes every door look honest."

Then laughter.

Then something else.

Not a compass.

A return piece.

Maybe.

No.

The word was close.

Backmark.

Door-mark.

Last mark.

The exact name would not come.

The function shape did.

You crossed a boundary.

It remembered one.

Then showed you back.

Useful in ruins.

Useful underground.

Useful in smoke.

Useful when every corridor looked the same.

And useless the moment you crossed the wrong doorway.

That last part arrived with the memory.

Important.

I wrote it down before confidence improved it:

AFTER TALLY DOOR -> POINTS BACK TO TALLY DOOR

CROSS DOOR -> CLICK + ORIENTATION CHANGES

POSSIBLE LAST-THRESHOLD RETURN PIECE

Then:

MEMORY SUPPORTS CATEGORY, NOT EXACT OBJECT

The dye woman at the worktable read upside down as I passed.

"You writing a book?"

"Trying not to."

I crossed the wooden door into the front hall.

Click.

I opened the case.

The oval now pointed back toward the wooden door.

Good.

Then I crossed the hanging cloth curtain.

No click.

The oval stayed pointed toward the wooden door.

Interesting.

Not every boundary.

Not cloth.

Maybe rigid frame.

Maybe enclosed threshold.

Maybe something magical in the door.

I stepped through the front shop door onto the street.

Click.

The oval rotated toward the shop entrance.

I smiled.

Then a cart nearly ran over my crutch tip because I was standing in a doorway staring at a small black object.

I moved.

Artifacts did not improve survival if you used them stupidly.

Good lesson.

I did not go home.

Not yet.

I walked two blocks with the oval case open inside my bag enough that I could glance down without touching it.

It continued to point roughly toward the dye-shop front door.

At the first alley I turned.

Still toward the shop.

At the second street I turned again.

Still.

No click.

Distance had not obviously erased it.

Useful.

Then I entered a bakery.

Click.

The oval rotated toward the bakery door.

I left immediately.

Click.

The oval rotated toward the same bakery door from outside.

I frowned.

That was different.

If it always pointed to the last crossed doorway, crossing back out should have made it point to the bakery door anyway.

Same physical threshold.

No contradiction.

I needed two doors.

The baker watched me through the window.

I bought nothing.

This was becoming socially expensive without costing money.

Across the street was a narrow public passage through an old counting house. One door on the south side, one on the north, corridor between. People used it as a shortcut.

Perfect.

I entered south.

Click.

Oval pointed south.

Crossed the north door.

Click.

Oval rotated north.

Good.

Then I stepped back through north.

Click.

Oval pointed north from inside.

Then exited south.

Click.

Oval pointed south.

Last physical threshold.

Strongly.

Maybe.

Enough to use carefully.

I was still writing when somebody said, "You going somewhere?"

I looked up.

A courier stood beside me with two sealed tubes under one arm.

"Eventually."

"Then stop standing in the passage."

Correct.

I moved.

That should have been the chapter.

Not literally.

Life did not know about chapters.

But I had learned a usable thing.

The object appeared to mark the most recent qualifying doorway crossed and orient back toward it.

That was enough for one day.

So naturally I got lost twenty minutes later.

Not dramatically lost.

Carrow did not suddenly become a maze.

I took a side route around a blocked drain repair near Bell Street and ended up at the rear entrance of an old storage court I had never used.

A chalk board at the corner said:

SOUTH WALK CLOSED

USE LOWER PASSAGE

The lower passage entrance was a stone arch descending beneath two connected warehouses.

I could have gone around another three streets.

My shoulders objected.

The lower passage had a handrail.

I chose the passage.

This was not artifact testing.

This was laziness with documentation.

I crossed the stone arch.

Click.

Oval pointed back toward daylight.

The passage descended twelve shallow steps, turned left, then split.

One branch had painted arrows.

The other had barrels.

I followed arrows.

Second arch.

Click.

The oval changed.

Third doorway, wooden frame without a door.

Click.

Changed again.

Then the arrows disappeared.

Of course.

A worker carrying rope came the other way.

"Bell Street?"

I asked.

"Up right, then left at white post."

"Thanks."

I went up right.

White post.

Left.

Then found two identical doors.

No signs.

One smelled faintly of grain.

The other smelled like wet stone.

I could have waited for someone.

Instead I looked at the oval.

It pointed behind me.

Toward the last wooden frame I had crossed.

Not toward either new door.

Good.

That was actually useful.

I retraced to the frame.

Click.

The oval now pointed back toward the room I had just left.

There was the limitation.

The second I crossed the frame, I had overwritten the previous mark.

If I kept using it to retreat one doorway at a time, fine.

If I crossed the wrong door while confused, the object would faithfully help me return to the wrong door.

Not a path recorder.

Not a route map.

One threshold.

One.

I remembered the old shelter woman again.

"Because dark makes every door look honest."

And someone else answering:

"It only remembers the last liar."

There.

Not the formal name.

But the joke.

I laughed in the underground passage by myself.

A man stacking crates looked at me.

"You all right?"

"Better than five minutes ago."

"Congratulations."

Carrow remained supportive.

I used the oval carefully after that.

Not to find Bell Street.

To preserve retreat.

Before crossing any uncertain doorway, I looked at where it pointed.

Then crossed.

If the next space was wrong, I could return one step.

This changed how I moved.

That was the first real proof that I had bought something other than curiosity.

Not power.

Procedure.

I stopped choosing doors casually.

Every doorway became a small decision because crossing it rewrote the only return marker I had.

The object made navigation safer and more annoying at the same time.

Good artifact.

Possibly.

I found Bell Street eight minutes later.

Outside, I sat on a low wall and wrote until my hand cramped.

OBSERVED QUALIFYING THRESHOLDS:

WOOD DOOR

STONE ARCH

OPEN WOOD FRAME

PUBLIC PASSAGE DOORS

NOT CLOTH CURTAIN

Then:

POINTS BACK TO MOST RECENT QUALIFYING THRESHOLD AFTER CROSSING

I stared at that sentence.

Too strong.

Changed it to:

SO FAR, CONSISTENT WITH MOST RECENT QUALIFYING THRESHOLD

Then:

CROSSING NEW QUALIFYING THRESHOLD OVERWRITES PRIOR ORIENTATION

That one had direct support.

At least four times.

Then:

USEFUL FOR ONE-STEP RETREAT

NOT ROUTE MEMORY

I underlined the second line.

That was the downside.

A good one.

Not deadly.

Potentially deadly if you trusted it beyond what it did.

Those were often the most dangerous tools.

I wrapped the oval again before heading home.

It clicked once when I entered the building.

I ignored it.

Then once at the apartment door.

I opened the case upstairs.

The oval pointed toward the apartment door.

Tavi was on the floor with wooden blocks.

"Treasure works?"

"A little."

He stood immediately.

"What does it do?"

"It remembers a door."

Lyssa looked over from the table.

"One door?"

"Apparently."

"Which door?"

"Last one."

"Useful."

"Sometimes."

"Bad?"

"Also sometimes."

She nodded.

That was all.

No applause.

Correct response.

I hung the oval from a short loop of spare cord through its tiny hole and suspended it from a wooden peg near my upstairs door.

Not touching the wall.

It rotated slowly until the narrow end aimed toward the doorway.

That felt closer to the first-life memory.

A black piece hanging beside a shelter door.

Not held flat.

Not boxed.

Free to turn.

I did not know whether hanging was required.

I only knew it made the behavior easier to see.

I wrote:

HANGING = EASIER TO READ

NOT PROVEN REQUIRED

Then I stopped.

The object had earned a name in my notes.

Not a real name.

A working one.

LAST-DOOR OVAL

Ugly.

Useful.

I could improve it later.

Or discover everybody else called it something obvious and feel stupid.

Both seemed likely.

I counted my money.

Two copper.

Still two.

The artifact had not made me richer.

It had made one kind of mistake cheaper.

That was better than I expected for one copper.

Then Tavi ran out of the room.

The oval clicked.

I looked at it.

He had not gone through my upstairs door.

He had crossed the open doorway into the hall.

The oval rotated toward it.

I frowned.

No physical door.

Just a frame.

Qualifying threshold.

Good.

Then Tavi came back through.

Click.

The oval still pointed toward the same frame.

Of course.

Same threshold.

I added one final note:

DOOR NOT REQUIRED

FRAME MAY BE ENOUGH

Then I put the charcoal down.

One layer.

Enough.

I had learned what the object could do today.

More importantly, I had learned what it could not do.

The first made it useful.

The second made it survivable.

# CHAPTER 328

## THE WRONG DOOR

The problem with knowing which door was behind you was that sometimes the door behind you was the problem.

I learned this at the theatre.

Of course I did.

The message came just after breakfast.

Not from Teren.

Not from Rinna.

Not even from Nessa.

A boy I recognized from the theatre's front steps knocked on our door, handed Cala a folded scrap, and said, "For Greg. They said if he's here."

Cala looked at me.

"You're here."

"Strong start."

The boy had already left.

The scrap said:

GREG

IF FREE BEFORE SECOND BELL

BACK HALL WALK

NEW STORAGE ROUTE

NESSA

No pay written.

No promise of work.

No emergency.

Just a route.

I smiled anyway.

Lyssa saw it.

"Theatre?"

"Maybe."

"You have theatre face."

"I don't have a theatre face."

"You do."

"What does it look like?"

"Like somebody remembered you."

That was rude enough that I folded the note and put it in my bag.

The last-door oval hung from its short cord near the upstairs doorway.

I looked at it.

Then at the bag.

Then back at it.

I had not planned to carry it every day.

That was how useful objects became habits before you understood their failure modes.

Also how people lost useful objects.

I took it anyway.

Not loose.

I wrapped it, put it in the shallow case, and tucked the case into the shoulder bag where it could not knock against the Kiln chit or my charcoal.

The holdfast stayed home.

Separate problems.

Still a good rule.

The theatre looked exactly like itself.

That was more comforting than I expected.

Front doors open.

Painted board crooked by a degree nobody else cared about.

A coil of rope near the wall that had probably been there for months and would outlive us all.

Someone inside shouted, "Not that bench."

Someone else shouted, "I know."

This was almost certainly false.

I crossed the front door.

Click.

The oval moved inside the case.

I did not stop to inspect it.

That was new too.

Useful things did not require applause every time they worked.

Nessa found me near the side aisle.

"You came."

"The note was persuasive."

"It had six words."

"Efficient persuasion."

She handed me a narrow wooden slat with a chalk mark on one end.

"Walk."

"Good morning."

"Morning. Walk."

There she was.

The theatre had changed its back storage route.

Not dramatically.

A rear property room had been partially emptied so a wall repair could happen next week. Until then, long objects that normally went through the rear hall had to move through a side passage, across the old wardrobe room, then behind the left stage wall.

The problem was the wardrobe-room turn.

It was tight.

The second problem was the new shelving someone had installed in the side passage.

It was also tight.

The third problem was Marek.

He was standing beside a long painted spear.

Nessa pointed at him.

"Do not help."

Marek put a hand to his chest.

"I have not done anything."

"Correct. Continue."

"Cruel management."

"Not management. Survival."

I took the wooden slat.

"What is this?"

"Length."

"Of?"

"The flower frame."

The flower frame was a tall narrow piece of scenery used in the garden sequence. Not heavy, but long enough to become an argument in every doorway.

Nessa had cut the slat to match its longest rigid dimension.

Smart.

"You want the route checked before moving it."

"I want you to walk the slat through without deciding the building should be wider."

"That limits my best solutions."

"Good."

Jori appeared from behind a flat carrying a hammer.

"Shelf corner catches at shoulder height."

"Whose shoulder?" I asked.

He looked at me.

"Not yours."

"Useful."

"Marek's."

Marek said, "My shoulders are being unfairly documented."

Nessa said, "Walk."

I walked.

The route began through the side-stage door.

Click.

Then the narrow service passage.

No threshold for several yards.

New shelving on the right.

Old wall on left.

The slat cleared.

At the wardrobe-room door, I turned sideways.

Click.

The slat cleared the frame but clipped a hanging coat inside.

I stopped.

"Object clears. Cloth doesn't."

Nessa, behind me, moved the coat hook two pegs farther in.

No discussion.

Good workplace.

Across the wardrobe room.

Second door.

Click.

Then left behind the stage wall.

I stopped.

"Clear if the frame stays upright until wardrobe, sideways inside, upright after second door."

Nessa nodded.

Marek said, "That sounds familiar."

"Because you learned it with flowers," Nessa said.

"I discovered it with flowers."

"You got stuck with flowers."

"Discovery often begins in adversity."

Jori handed him the spear.

"Discover somewhere else."

The oval had clicked three times.

Front entrance.

Side-stage door.

Wardrobe-room door.

Then second wardrobe door.

Four, actually.

I had stopped counting automatically.

That should have been good.

Except the new route had just demonstrated the object's weakness better than any alley could.

If I needed to retreat from behind the stage wall, the oval would point me back through the second wardrobe door.

Fine.

Once I crossed it, the first wardrobe door became the remembered threshold.

Fine.

One step at a time.

But if somebody opened another qualifying framed access along the way and I crossed it by mistake, the useful retreat point disappeared.

The theatre was full of doors.

Backstage was basically architecture trying to create mistakes.

Nessa took the slat.

"Again with the actual frame."

The flower frame arrived with Jori on one end and Davin on the other.

I stepped aside.

"Where do you want me?"

Nessa pointed ahead.

"Wardrobe. Call the turn."

That was familiar enough.

I went ahead.

Side-stage door.

Click.

Service passage.

Wardrobe door.

Click.

I positioned myself inside the wardrobe room where I could see both ends of the turn.

"Straight."

The flower frame entered.

"Stop."

Jori stopped.

Davin stopped half a beat later.

"Top right close. Lower left clear. Rotate toward me."

They rotated.

The painted flowers passed the moved coat hook by two inches.

"Good. Keep."

Marek appeared in the other doorway.

Of course.

"Need me to take the front?"

Nessa's voice came from behind the frame.

"No."

"I could."

"Continue not helping."

He leaned against the second doorframe.

The frame came through.

Jori lifted his end.

Davin matched.

Clear.

Easy.

Then someone shouted from the stage.

Not panic.

Urgency.

"Nessa!"

She answered, "What?"

"Rain side's in."

Nessa swore once.

Specific problem.

The rain side was a painted weather flat stored near the rear wall.

If water had gotten into the damaged back room, the wall repair had apparently started early without permission from weather.

Nessa pointed at Jori and Davin.

"Frame to left storage. Greg, with me. Marek, don't touch anything wet."

"That is too broad."

"Good."

We moved.

Fast for me.

Which meant everybody else moved at a pace that did not make me want to murder them.

That was belonging too.

Nobody announced it.

They just did not leave me behind.

We crossed back through the wardrobe-room door.

Click.

Then the first door.

Click.

Then side-stage.

Click.

The oval was now remembering a door I could see behind me.

Very useful.

We reached the rear hall.

Water had come under the outer service door and spread along one wall.

Not flood water.

A hard wind had driven rain through a gap around temporary boards outside.

The rain-side flat leaned against the wall with its lower edge darkening.

Nessa said, "Lift bottom."

Two workers grabbed it.

I took the nearest loose cloth bundle off the floor and moved it onto a bench.

"Not that one," Nessa said.

I stopped.

"Why?"

"Wet dye."

I put it on a different bench.

"Excellent time to learn."

"That's why I said it."

Jori and Davin arrived without the flower frame.

Good.

Jori looked at the water.

"Board seam."

Davin said, "Outside?"

"Has to be."

Nessa pointed.

"Check."

They went through the rear service door.

Click.

I had not crossed it.

The oval still clicked.

I froze.

That was new.

Nessa was already moving the next object.

I almost ignored the sound.

Then the oval clicked again.

Soft.

Inside my bag.

Nobody had crossed near me.

I opened the case.

The oval was turning.

Toward the rear service door.

I stared.

I had not crossed it.

That broke the rule.

Or improved it.

Or revealed that my rule had been wrong from the beginning.

"Greg."

Nessa.

I closed the case.

"Coming."

Work first.

Mystery later.

We moved two rolled backcloths, one crate of painted cups, and a basket of costume trim away from the wet wall.

The water line stopped growing.

Outside, Jori and Davin shoved something heavy against the temporary board seam.

Someone inside fetched rags.

Marek arrived carrying three dry ones.

Nessa looked at him.

"Those dry?"

"Painfully."

"Good. Floor."

He put them down.

Useful.

No disaster.

Just work.

Then the rear service door slammed shut in the wind.

The oval clicked hard enough that I felt it through the bag.

Not loud.

Sharper.

I opened the case again.

The narrow end pointed toward the rear service door.

I had still not crossed it.

I looked at the door.

Then at the oval.

Then at Nessa.

"Who went through there last?"

"Jori and Davin."

"Before them?"

"Why?"

"Humor me."

She thought.

"Teren earlier. Maybe Venn. Why?"

"Not enough."

"Greg."

"Later."

She accepted that because the floor was wet and unlike me, Nessa had priorities.

Jori opened the rear door from outside.

"Seam's blocked for now. Need someone to tell Rinna the outside boards are wrong."

"I'll go," Nessa said.

She turned.

The oval rotated slightly.

Not toward her.

Toward the door.

Good.

Not person tracking.

Probably.

I looked at the threshold.

I had not crossed it.

But the object behaved as if it had become relevant anyway.

Why?

The memory came back sideways.

Not the shelter.

A ruin.

First life.

Smoke.

Three doors in a stone corridor.

A scout named Pel had tied a black return piece to his belt.

I remembered mocking him because he had walked through the wrong arch and overwritten it.

Then later, when half the corridor collapsed, he had thrown the piece through a doorway before crossing.

No.

Not thrown.

Someone else had carried it.

The memory blurred.

But there had been an argument.

"It marks the crossing," I had said.

Pel had answered something.

Not crossing.

Passage.

Use.

Claim.

I could not recover the word.

Jori and Davin had crossed it.

The oval was in my bag.

So why would their crossing matter?

Unless the artifact was not keyed to me.

That possibility was much worse.

I took the oval out by its cord.

Nessa saw.

Click.

Click.

"Yes."

"Unknown."

"Annoying?"

"Extremely."

Fair.

He inspected the rear boards.

Nobody asked me about the oval.

Also good.

I stayed another hour because the new storage route still needed walking after the rain-side interruption.

No one offered pay.

I had not come for pay.

That mattered less than it once would have.

Not because I had money.

Two copper was not wealth.

Because this was a place where a six-word note could bring me in to check a route before somebody moved the actual frame.

That had value too.

Different ledger.

Side-stage door.

Click when I crossed.

Wardrobe door.

Click when I crossed.

Second wardrobe door.

Click when I crossed.

No surprise.

No click.

Good.

Marek crossed the same opening.

No click.

Also good.

That made the rear door stranger.

I wrote only:

REAR SERVICE DOOR UPDATED WITHOUT ME CROSSING

J + D CROSSED / NOT ENOUGH TO CLAIM CAUSE

LATER NESSA + MAREK CROSSINGS NEAR ME -> NO UPDATE

Then I stopped.

Nessa read over my shoulder.

"You write like Rinna."

"That is the meanest thing anyone has said to me today."

From across the room Rinna said, "I can hear you."

"Then it worked."

She did not look up from the carpenter's note.

Home by late afternoon.

The oval had behaved normally the entire walk back.

Every qualifying threshold I crossed replaced the last.

No unexplained updates.

At the apartment, I crossed the front door.

Click.

Building door.

Click.

Upstairs doorway.

Click.

I hung the oval from its short cord.

It pointed back toward the upstairs frame.

Tavi came in.

No click.

Lyssa came in.

No click.

Cala passed the doorway twice.

Nothing.

Good.

I sat on the floor with the narrow scrap.

The rear service door bothered me.

Not because it broke the rule.

Because it suggested a second rule.

And second rules were where useful artifacts became expensive mistakes.

I went through my memory again.

Pel.

Smoke.

Collapsed corridor.

Black piece.

Argument.

He had said...

"You don't mark the door," I whispered.

Lyssa looked over from the table.

"What?"

I held up a finger.

The memory came.

Not all of it.

Enough.

Pel had been angry because I called it a last-door marker.

"It doesn't remember doors," he had said.

"It remembers retreat."

I stared at the oval.

That was different.

Maybe.

A door I crossed was an obvious retreat threshold.

But the rear service door had become the only useful retreat from a wet, blocked work area when Jori and Davin went outside and the wind shut it.

Had the artifact selected it because the situation changed?

That sounded too intelligent.

Too convenient.

Too much like turning one strange observation into a miracle.

I wrote:

FIRST-LIFE MEMORY: `REMEMBERS RETREAT` ?

Then beneath it:

DO NOT TRUST WORDING YET

Lyssa said, "Good rule."

"You weren't invited."

"You said it out loud."

"Household espionage."

The oval turned slowly on its cord.

Not toward the doorway.

Away from it.

I stopped breathing for half a second.

Then it continued turning.

Past the wall.

Past the window.

Until its narrow end pointed toward the stairs.

The upstairs doorway was behind it now.

No one had crossed anything.

I stood.

"Lyssa."

She looked up.

The oval clicked.

Downstairs, somebody screamed.

Not theatrical.

Not playful.

A real scream.

I grabbed both crutches.

The oval pointed toward the stairs.

And for the first time, I did not know whether it was showing me the way back.

Or the way out.

# CHAPTER 329

## THE WAY OUT

The scream came from downstairs.

The oval pointed toward the stairs.

I trusted the scream.

I did not trust the oval.

That seemed like the correct order.

I grabbed both crutches and moved.

Urgency on two crutches was not running.

It was committing harder to every placement.

Right crutch.

Left crutch.

Right foot.

Down.

Again.

The first stair was always the worst because my body wanted speed and the geometry wanted honesty.

Lyssa was behind me.

"Who was that?"

"Don't know."

"Tavi?"

"Don't know."

She hated the second answer more.

So did I.

The oval hung from its cord in my left hand because putting it back in the bag would have cost seconds and dropping it would have been stupid.

It pointed down the stairwell.

Not perfectly.

Roughly.

Enough to annoy me.

At the first landing, the front half of the building smelled wrong.

Not smoke.

Hot metal.

Wet plaster.

Something sharp underneath.

I stopped.

Lyssa nearly hit me.

"What?"

"Smell."

Then another voice yelled from below.

Cala.

"Back! Back from the wall!"

Good.

Cala was alive.

That removed one terrible possibility.

Not the others.

I moved again.

The oval clicked.

I had crossed the landing frame.

Normal.

It rotated toward the frame behind me.

Also normal.

Then, halfway down the next flight, it turned in my hand.

Away from the frame.

Toward the rear of the building.

No threshold crossed.

I almost stopped.

Did not.

Scream first.

Artifact later.

At the ground floor, Tavi stood near the kitchen doorway holding both hands over his ears.

Alive.

Unhurt.

Cala had one arm across his chest keeping him back.

The scream had come from the woman next door.

Neris.

She was in the shared front hall barefoot, staring at a section of wall beside the building entrance.

The plaster there had split open.

Not a crack.

Opened.

A wedge-shaped chunk had fallen outward onto the floor, exposing blackened lath and a narrow metal pipe behind it.

The pipe glowed dull orange at one joint.

No flame.

Yet.

Neris pointed at it.

"It hissed."

The pipe hissed again.

Everyone moved back.

Good instincts.

A bead of pale light formed along the joint.

Then ran upward instead of down.

Bad sign.

I knew this category.

Not the local installation.

Heat line.

Service line.

Something carrying more than ordinary hot water.

Old Greg had lived in enough buildings to know you did not touch glowing wall pipes with cloth and optimism.

"Rear out," I said.

Cala looked at me.

"Why?"

Because the oval was pointing rear.

Bad answer.

Because the front wall contained a glowing service line beside the main entrance.

Good answer.

"Front entrance is beside the line. Rear is farther from it."

Cala nodded immediately.

"Tavi. Shoes."

"No time," I said.

"Floor's stone."

"Still no time."

Tavi already had one shoe in his hand somehow.

Children could manifest the wrong object under pressure with impressive consistency.

Lyssa grabbed a folded blanket from the bench.

Cala said, "Leave it."

Lyssa left it.

Also good.

Neris looked toward her own door.

"My papers."

"No," Cala said.

Neris took one step anyway.

The pipe joint popped.

Not exploded.

Popped.

The pale bead of light vanished.

A line of heat shimmer spread across the exposed metal.

Neris stopped wanting papers.

We moved rear.

The building's back route was worse than the front on a normal day.

Narrow kitchen passage.

Small storage turn.

Rear service door into the courtyard.

I had crossed all of it hundreds of times.

The oval hung in front of me.

It pointed toward the rear service door.

That was the same direction I already wanted.

Which made it useless as evidence and useful as comfort.

Annoying combination.

Cala went first with Tavi.

Neris behind her.

Lyssa waited for me.

"Go," I said.

"No."

"I'm slower."

"Yes."

"That was not permission to agree."

"Move."

We moved.

The storage turn was tight enough that I had to shorten both crutches and angle one forward.

Not literally shorten them.

There was no miracle hinge.

I choked my grip higher and used less swing.

My right shoulder complained from yesterday's theatre work.

Today it lost the vote.

Behind us, something struck the front hall wall.

Heavy.

Maybe more plaster.

Maybe the pipe support.

No flame sound.

No scream.

Keep moving.

Cala opened the rear service door.

The oval clicked before I crossed it.

Everyone else had already gone through.

I stopped for half a heartbeat.

There.

Again.

Update before my crossing.

Lyssa saw me stop.

"Greg."

"Moving."

I crossed.

Click again.

The oval rotated back toward the rear service door from the courtyard.

Normal after crossing.

We were out.

All of us.

Neris.

Cala.

Tavi.

Lyssa.

Me.

No one burned.

No one crushed.

No one heroically carried furniture.

Excellent evacuation.

The courtyard was already filling with people from the other units.

Someone from upstairs had heard Cala yelling and come down the rear stair.

A man from the next building shouted, "Heat line?"

Cala answered, "Wall joint. Front hall."

He ran toward the street instead of the building.

Good man.

Probably fetching someone who knew more.

The oval pointed at the rear service door.

I did not need it anymore.

Then the front windows flashed white.

Not fire.

A hard white pulse behind the glass.

Everyone ducked anyway.

A second later, the front door slammed open by itself.

Steam rolled out low along the floor.

Not ordinary steam.

Too bright.

Tiny pale sparks moved inside it and vanished when they touched stone.

Charge steam.

Maybe.

Local name unknown.

Whatever it was, I was suddenly even happier to be in the courtyard.

Tavi said, "Cool."

Cala said, "No."

"But it is."

"No."

Strong household doctrine.

A municipal response cart arrived faster than expected.

Not instantly.

Fast enough that someone nearby had probably known exactly which bell chain to pull.

Two workers in gray coats came through the courtyard gate carrying long red-handled tools and a folded black mat.

A third went to the street side.

No one asked me to help.

Perfect.

The lead worker said, "Anyone inside?"

Cala counted us aloud.

Not names.

Numbers.

Then pointed at Neris.

"Her unit shares the front wall. Everyone from ours is out. Upper rear came through courtyard. Front upstairs unknown."

Useful.

The worker shouted toward the street.

Another voice answered, "Clearing now."

The black mat went across the rear threshold.

One worker pressed a red-handled tool against the courtyard-side wall.

The handle lit amber.

He said, "Line still carrying."

The other worker swore.

Technical language transcended professions.

They did not enter through the rear.

Instead they moved around to the front.

Interesting.

I looked at the oval.

It still pointed toward the rear service door.

Which was now the door we had just used to escape.

Fine.

Consistent.

But before crossing, it had pointed there too.

That mattered more.

Maybe.

Neris was shaking.

Not dramatically.

Hands mostly.

Cala took her elbow.

"Sit."

"My papers."

"Still no."

"They're from my mother."

Cala's expression changed.

Not enough to let her go back in.

"We'll see after."

Neris nodded.

Sat on an overturned crate.

Tavi stood beside her with one bare foot and one shoe.

He looked at the shoe.

Then at his foot.

Then put the shoe down without putting it on.

I did not ask.

Some mysteries belonged to children.

Lyssa looked at the oval.

"It pointed back here before we crossed."

"Yes."

"That seems less like last door."

"Yes."

"More like retreat."

I hated that she had used the word first.

"Maybe."

"You remember something?"

"A phrase. Not enough."

"Good."

Apparently everyone in my life had become Hessa.

The municipal workers came back around after several minutes.

The lead one had soot on one sleeve.

"Line's isolated."

Cala asked, "Fire?"

"No sustained flame. Joint failed inside wall. Pressure cooked the plaster and vented through the hall."

"Cause?"

"Not yet."

Good answer.

"Can we go in?"

"Rear only. One at a time. Don't touch front wall. Don't open front units until we clear them."

Neris stood.

"My papers."

The worker pointed at her door.

"Front wall unit?"

"Yes."

"Not yet."

She sat again.

Cala asked, "Our kitchen?"

"Rear side is clear enough to enter and collect essentials. No staying inside until inspection."

There it was.

We were temporarily out of our own apartment.

Not homeless.

Not disaster.

Enough to become annoying quickly.

Cala looked at me.

"Can you get shoes?"

I looked at Tavi.

One bare foot.

"Apparently necessary."

The municipal worker said, "One person. Rear route only."

Cala started to volunteer.

I said, "I'll do it."

Everyone looked at me.

I regretted speaking.

"Why you?" Cala asked.

Because the oval had just led rear before we crossed.

Again bad answer.

"I know exactly where his shoes are likely not to be."

Tavi said, "One is upstairs."

"See? Strong intelligence."

Cala frowned.

"You were just moving fast on stairs."

"I'm fine."

Lyssa said, "He is."

Traitor.

The worker looked at my crutches.

"Rear stair dry?"

Cala said, "Yes."

"Then one trip. Essentials only. If you smell hot metal stronger, turn around. If the rear wall warms, turn around. If you see pale light in plaster, turn around."

"Good list."

"Not a challenge."

"Understood."

I went back in.

This time the oval mattered.

Not because I trusted it over the municipal worker.

Because retreat had become an actual operational concern.

I crossed the rear service door.

Click.

Oval pointed back to courtyard.

Good.

Kitchen passage.

Storage turn.

No new qualifying threshold.

Rear stair door.

Click.

Now the oval pointed back to the stair door.

There was the limitation.

The courtyard was no longer the remembered retreat.

One-step only.

I knew that.

I still disliked it.

Up the stairs.

My pace slower now.

Urgency without adrenaline pretending gravity had resigned.

The air smelled normal on the rear side.

At the upstairs doorway, click.

Oval updated.

Courtyard gone.

Stair door gone.

Only upstairs doorway remained.

This object was not safety.

It was breadcrumbs if you agreed to eat every old crumb when you dropped a new one.

Useful.

Dangerous if misunderstood.

I found Tavi's second shoe under the table.

Of course.

Then grabbed Cala's small document tin because essentials meant essentials and because she would pretend not to want it until later.

Lyssa's dark work stayed.

My holdfast stayed.

The basket of repair junk stayed.

I looked at the holdfast.

Two-copper object.

Unknown.

Mine.

Not essential during a service-line evacuation.

Good.

Then the oval turned.

Not toward the upstairs doorway.

Toward the window.

I stopped.

No scream this time.

No white flash.

No obvious danger.

Just the oval rotating slowly toward the window.

I did not follow it.

The worker had said rear route only.

Window was not route.

Maybe it was pointing at open air.

Maybe toward the courtyard beyond the wall.

Maybe toward something else entirely.

I wrote nothing.

Not now.

I took the shoe and document tin.

Crossed the upstairs doorway.

Click.

The oval pointed back to it.

Normal.

Down the stairs.

Rear stair door.

Click.

Updated.

Kitchen passage.

Rear service door.

Click.

Updated.

Courtyard.

Done.

The municipal worker checked what I carried.

"That's it?"

"Shoe and documents."

He looked at Tavi.

"Good priorities."

Tavi took the shoe.

"I knew where it was."

"You said upstairs."

"It was."

Technically correct.

The inspection took most of the afternoon.

The front hall wall was opened wider.

The failed joint belonged to an old building heat-service run embedded through the front partition. Exact cause stayed unknown. The workers said they needed a linewright before restoring service.

No sustained fire.

No structural evacuation beyond the building for now.

We could sleep inside if the rear route remained clear and the front hall stayed closed off.

Neris eventually got her papers after a worker entered with her.

She cried harder when she came back out holding them than she had during the failure.

Nobody commented.

Good neighbors.

By evening, temporary black boards covered the opened wall section.

A red chalk line marked where nobody was supposed to stand.

Tavi stepped over it once.

Cala moved him back without words.

He stayed back.

Progress.

The oval hung upstairs again.

Not beside the doorway this time.

I moved its cord to a hook where I could see both the upstairs doorway and the window.

Lyssa sat on the bed edge.

"So?"

"So what?"

"It pointed toward the way out before we crossed it."

"Yes."

"Then later it pointed at the window."

I looked at her.

"You saw?"

"No. Your face did."

Unfair.

I took out the narrow scrap.

Under the Ch328 note I wrote:

HOUSE LINE FAILURE

OVAL TURNED TO REAR ROUTE BEFORE MY CROSSING

REAR = ACTUAL SAFER EXIT GIVEN FRONT-WALL FAILURE

Then I stopped.

The sentence was too strong.

I crossed out `SAFER`.

Wrote:

REAR = EXIT WE USED / FRONT BESIDE FAILED LINE

Better.

Then:

INSIDE RETURN TRIP: NORMAL LAST-THRESHOLD OVERWRITE

UPSTAIRS OVAL TURNED TOWARD WINDOW WITHOUT CROSSING / NO EVENT OBSERVED

Lyssa read it.

"You think it knows escape routes."

"I think I want it to."

"Different."

"Very."

The first-life phrase sat below everything:

REMEMBERS RETREAT ?

I stared at it.

Retreat could mean last threshold.

Retreat could mean current viable exit.

Retreat could mean whichever direction had been used as retreat before.

Retreat could be a terrible translation of a technical word I remembered emotionally instead of correctly.

Old Greg had known how to use dozens of things he could no longer name cleanly.

That was embarrassing.

Also realistic.

I added:

DOES NOT = SAFE PATH

Then underlined it.

Because even today, the object had pointed toward the rear route before we crossed it.

That had been useful.

Later it pointed at a window I was not supposed to use.

Also useful.

Not because the window was right.

Because it stopped me from turning a helpful artifact into an authority.

The oval rotated on its cord.

Slowly.

Toward the upstairs doorway.

Normal again.

I smiled.

Lyssa said, "What?"

"Nothing."

"You have artifact face."

"I don't have an artifact face."

"You do."

"What does it look like?"

"Like you bought trouble and are happy it came with instructions."

I looked at the oval.

Then at the red chalk line visible through the stair opening below.

"Instructions would be generous."

"Warnings, then."

That was closer.

For one copper, I had bought a thing that sometimes remembered the last way back and sometimes, maybe, suggested a way out.

The difference between those two functions was large enough to get somebody killed.

So I wrote one final line:

USEFUL ENOUGH TO CARRY

NOT TRUSTED ENOUGH TO OBEY

That felt right.

For now.

# CHAPTER 330

## THE BACK DOOR

For three days, our front door became decorative.

This improved it.

No one knocked on it.

No one stood in it talking while everyone else tried to pass.

No one opened it and discovered Tavi directly behind them for reasons known only to Tavi.

The municipal workers had boarded the damaged section of the front hall, chalked a red line across the floor, and declared the entire front route closed until the linewright finished deciding whose fault the wall was.

Cala had asked when that would be.

The worker had said, "When he knows."

She had stared at him.

He had added, "Probably tomorrow."

It was now the day after tomorrow.

Civilization.

We used the rear service route instead.

Kitchen passage.

Storage turn.

Rear stair.

Courtyard.

Then around the building to the street.

It added perhaps forty seconds for a person with two good legs.

For me it added more.

Not much more.

Enough that I noticed every single time.

The rear stair was narrower than the front one and had a turn halfway down where the inside crutch had to land closer to the wall than I liked.

The first morning I hated it.

The second morning I had a pattern.

Right crutch.

Right foot.

Left crutch down one.

Turn hip.

Do not catch shoulder bag on the peg beside the landing.

The third morning, Tavi moved the peg.

I stopped halfway down.

"Why?"

He looked at the peg in his hand.

"You hit it."

"Once."

"Twice."

"That is slander."

He put it on a lower hole where it no longer caught the bag.

Then continued downstairs.

I stood there for a moment.

Belonging was apparently people altering architecture because you were annoying.

I liked it.

The oval clicked when I crossed the rear service door into the courtyard.

I barely looked.

That was progress too.

It lived in the shoulder bag now.

Not because I trusted it.

Because an object that had been useful twice earned pocket space.

Case space.

Whatever.

I still kept it wrapped.

Still did not press the mark.

Still did not channel mana into it.

Still did not ask it what I should have for breakfast.

High standards.

The building changed socially before it changed physically.

People who had used the front stair for years suddenly met in the courtyard.

Neris met the old man from the upper rear unit and discovered they had both been living ten feet apart without knowing each other's names.

Cala learned that the woman across the courtyard had been borrowing our rear wall to judge whether her own kitchen was warm enough in winter.

Nobody understood what that meant.

The woman refused to explain.

Tavi found three children who normally entered from the street side and immediately turned the rear route into a race.

Cala ended that within four minutes.

"No running on the rear stair."

"We weren't running," Tavi said.

"Then whatever faster thing you invented is also banned."

Strong law.

The linewright finally arrived near noon.

I knew because Cala called upstairs.

"Greg."

I looked up from the narrow scrap.

"What?"

"The wall man is here."

"Linewright."

"Wall man."

"You are going to offend a profession."

"Good. Come listen so I don't have to remember it."

That was not an invitation to investigate.

It was household administration.

Different danger.

The linewright was a woman.

Cala did not apologize.

She was perhaps fifty, broad through the shoulders, with gray hair braided close to her head and a dark red leather roll under one arm.

No uniform.

A small brass badge at her collar showed three nested squares around a dot.

Formal meaning unknown.

She stood behind the red chalk line looking at the opened wall.

Two municipal workers were with her.

One I recognized from the evacuation.

He recognized me enough to nod.

Good level of fame.

The linewright said, "Who owns the building?"

Cala named a man I had heard before and immediately forgotten.

The linewright wrote it down.

"Resident manager?"

"No."

"Rent collected where?"

Cala named a shop two streets away.

Written down.

"Any heat trouble before failure?"

Cala said, "Not in our unit."

Neris, from her doorway, said, "Mine clicked."

The linewright turned.

"What clicked?"

"Wall. Sometimes."

"When?"

Neris frowned.

"Cold mornings."

"This season?"

"Last season too."

"How often?"

"Not every day."

The linewright wrote.

No accusation.

No dramatic revelation.

Just information becoming expensive somewhere else.

She unrolled the dark red leather case on a crate.

Inside were four tools.

One looked like a flattened tuning fork.

One like a short black rod with a white ceramic tip.

One was a coil of thin copper-colored wire around a bone handle.

The last was a small square frame holding stretched translucent film.

Artifact-adjacent equipment.

Probably.

Specialist tools.

Definitely.

I stayed behind the chalk line.

Useful sentence.

The linewright held the square frame near the opened plaster.

The film tightened.

A pale orange line appeared across it.

She moved left.

The line bent.

Moved right.

Straightened.

One municipal worker said, "Seat?"

"Maybe."

Good answer.

She switched to the ceramic-tipped rod and touched exposed stone beside the failed joint.

Nothing happened.

Then touched the metal housing around the line.

The white ceramic went gray.

"Old load mark," she said.

"From failure?" the worker asked.

"Maybe older."

Even better answer.

I liked her.

Cala did not.

"Can we use the front door?"

The linewright looked at her.

"No."

"When?"

"After I know whether opening that wall farther makes the line worse."

"Today?"

"Probably."

Cala narrowed her eyes.

The linewright added, "Actually probably."

Improvement.

I looked at the oval inside my bag.

Not physically.

Mentally.

This was exactly the kind of moment where a stupid version of me would pull it out and say, `My mystery object pointed toward the rear before your wall exploded. Thoughts?`

Then I would become the interesting resident.

Never become the interesting resident during infrastructure repair.

I had learned things.

The linewright worked.

I went upstairs.

Two hours later, someone knocked on the rear service door.

That sentence felt wrong.

The rear door had not been a social door before.

It was for deliveries, rubbish, people carrying things that dripped, and household members avoiding the front.

Now it had become the only door.

I was closest.

I opened it.

Senna stood in the courtyard holding a flat board under one arm.

"This feels illegal," she said.

"It should."

"Your front door is boarded."

"We improved it."

She looked past me at the rear passage.

"Can I come in?"

The oval clicked inside my bag.

I had crossed nothing.

I froze.

Senna noticed.

"Was that you?"

"Unfortunately no."

The oval moved.

I could feel the case shift against my side.

Toward the courtyard behind Senna.

Or toward the rear service door.

Same line from where I stood.

Not useful yet.

I stepped backward into the kitchen passage without crossing another frame.

The oval stayed oriented toward the rear door.

Senna said, "Should I leave?"

"No. Why are you here?"

"Cala asked for a sign."

Of course she had.

Cala appeared behind me.

"Good."

Senna held up the board.

"You said rear entrance."

"Yes."

"You did not say how much rear entrance."

The board was perhaps two feet wide.

Painted in blue letters:

FRONT CLOSED

USE COURTYARD DOOR

Under that, smaller:

NO DELIVERIES THROUGH FRONT

Cala pointed at the last line.

"Good."

Senna looked at me.

"She pays better than you."

"Everyone does."

Cala took the board.

"How much?"

"One bit."

Cala paid her.

There.

A market price.

Not mine.

Senna saw my expression.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You made a money face."

Apparently this was visible across professions.

"I paid one copper for garbage recently."

"Bad garbage?"

"Promising garbage."

"Worse."

Cala carried the sign toward the courtyard.

Senna stayed.

"I brought the drawing."

I looked at the flat board under her arm.

"Which drawing?"

She gave me a look.

Right.

Me.

The portrait.

The one-copper portrait I had not bought.

She turned the board around.

It was not the original.

Smaller.

A copy.

Charcoal on cheap stiff paper, fixed lightly enough that it would still smudge if treated badly.

Me seated.

Crutches.

Bad hair.

Tired eyes.

That almost-joke in the mouth.

"Why?" I asked.

"The original sold."

I blinked.

"To who?"

"Woman from the square."

"Which woman?"

"The one who bought it."

Excellent provenance.

"For one copper?"

"No."

"How much?"

"Two bits."

I stared.

Senna smiled.

"You look offended."

"My face depreciated."

"Your face had no market."

"Cruel."

"She wanted the street studies together. Basket boy, old man, onion woman, you. I sold four for seven bits."

That was interesting.

Not because I was famous.

Because the portrait had value as part of a set that had nothing to do with me.

Good.

"So why copy mine?"

"Practice. Also you wanted it."

I looked at her.

"How much?"

"One bit."

I laughed.

She frowned.

"Too much?"

"I have zero bits."

"You have copper."

"Yes."

"Then change one."

I stopped.

That was embarrassingly obvious.

Not because conversion was obvious.

We still had not established one.

Because she was telling me to go get change somewhere, not that one copper equaled some invented number of bits.

"Where?"

"Any money table."

"At what rate?"

"Depends who is changing and how much."

There it was.

Useful and annoying.

"I am not changing a copper to buy my own face."

"Then don't."

"You could take copper and owe me."

"No."

"Strong business."

"I learned from the old man who sells garbage."

I stared.

"You know him?"

"No."

"Good."

She looked confused.

Better.

I looked at the copy again.

One bit.

I wanted it.

Still.

Maybe more now because the original had left the square.

But not enough to break a copper just to create small money today.

That was a choice.

Not inability.

"Keep it," I said.

Senna shrugged.

"Fine."

No tragedy.

No lesson.

She slid it back under her arm.

Then the oval clicked again.

Sharper.

Senna heard it this time.

"That definitely wasn't you."

"Correct."

The case moved against my hip.

I opened the bag.

Senna stepped back immediately.

Good instincts.

"Is that the garbage?"

"Promising garbage."

I took the shallow case out and opened it.

The oval pointed toward the rear service door.

Still.

"What does it do?"

"Sometimes it tells me where I should have gone."

"Useful."

"Sometimes."

Senna moved to the side.

The oval did not follow her.

Good.

Cala came back through the courtyard door carrying the sign's old wrapping cloth.

The oval clicked.

Turned.

Not toward Cala.

Toward the kitchen passage behind me.

I stared.

Cala stopped.

"What?"

"Nothing proven."

"Good."

Senna said, "Everyone says that to you?"

"I have cultivated a reputation."

The oval now pointed deeper into the apartment.

Not at the rear exit.

That seemed wrong if it was selecting retreat from danger.

Unless there was no danger.

Which there wasn't.

Probably.

So perhaps `retreat` was not emergency at all.

Maybe it was simply the most useful reversible boundary under current movement.

That sentence was terrible.

I did not write it.

Senna left through the rear door.

Click.

The oval did not update toward her.

Cala crossed into the kitchen.

Nothing.

I crossed the kitchen doorway.

Click.

The oval pointed back.

Normal.

Fine.

I put it away.

Not every click deserved a chapter.

That afternoon, the linewright opened more of the wall.

This produced dust, three new boards, and a phrase I immediately disliked.

"Building-side seat failure."

Cala said, "Meaning?"

The linewright sat back on her heels.

"Meaning the city feed is carrying correctly to the wall. The receiving seat in the building failed under load."

"Whose responsibility?"

"Probably owner."

There it was.

The important magic.

Liability.

Cala's shoulders dropped half an inch.

Not because she wanted the owner punished.

Because `probably owner` meant `probably not residents paying directly today.`

Probably.

I understood that feeling deeply.

"How long?" Cala asked.

"Temporary bypass by evening if the owner authorizes. Proper seat replacement after."

"If he doesn't authorize?"

The linewright looked at the opened wall.

"Then he can explain to his tenants why they don't have front heat service."

Cala smiled.

The owner authorized.

Amazing what concentrated inconvenience could accomplish.

By sunset, a temporary black conduit ran visibly along the upper front-hall wall instead of inside it.

Ugly.

Functional.

The red keep-clear line remained around the opened section.

Front door reopened with instructions not to lean anything against the temporary conduit and not to touch the sealed wall housing.

Tavi asked whether he could look.

The linewright said yes.

He asked whether he could touch.

She said no.

He asked why.

She crouched to his height and said, "Because it can burn you."

He nodded.

Best technical explanation of the day.

Then she stood and looked at my crutches.

Not rudely.

Practically.

"Rear stair working for you?"

"Less badly now."

"Front route will stay open unless the bypass heats. If it heats, don't wait for a worker. Use rear and pull the courtyard bell."

"What counts as heats?"

"Too warm to keep your palm near the wall for three breaths. Don't touch the conduit itself."

Specific.

Good.

"Any sound?"

"Fast ticking. Repeating. One click by itself means nothing."

I looked at my bag.

She noticed.

"What?"

"I own something that clicks."

"Then don't use it to diagnose my line."

I liked her even more.

"Wasn't planning to."

"Good."

She packed her tools.

No artifact conversation.

No appraisal.

No destiny.

Just a woman who knew her wall.

That night we used the front stairs again.

I had become accustomed to the rear route quickly enough that the front felt too wide.

Tavi ran halfway up before Cala said his name.

He stopped.

Walked.

Progress survived architecture.

At the upstairs doorway, the oval clicked.

Normal.

I hung it from the hook.

It pointed back toward the doorway.

Also normal.

Lyssa sat at the table with the dark cloth again.

"Front fixed?"

"Temporarily."

"Good."

"Senna came."

"I know."

"How?"

"Cala told me."

"Household espionage."

"Did you buy the drawing?"

"No."

"How much?"

"One bit."

"You have copper."

"Everyone keeps saying that."

"Because you do."

I sat.

"I didn't want it enough to go change money."

Lyssa looked at me for a second.

"That's different."

"Yes."

No praise.

Good.

I took out the narrow scrap.

Under the house-line notes I wrote:

BUILDING-SIDE SEAT FAILURE

TEMP BYPASS / OWNER AUTHORIZED

FRONT OPEN AGAIN

Then:

SENNA COPY 1 BIT / DECLINED

I stared at that.

Not because it mattered economically.

Because it did.

A month ago, `I cannot buy this` and `I choose not to buy this` had lived too close together.

Now they were separating.

Two copper did not make me rich.

It made some decisions mine.

I liked that.

The oval turned on its cord.

I watched it without moving.

It rotated perhaps ten degrees.

Then stopped.

No click.

No scream.

No wall burst.

Nothing happened.

I waited.

Still nothing.

Then Tavi came through the doorway carrying the wooden spoon again.

Click.

The oval pointed back toward the door.

He looked at it.

"Treasure?"

"Useful garbage."

He nodded as if that made perfect sense.

Maybe it did.

Downstairs, someone opened the restored front door.

The temporary conduit gave one ordinary settling tick.

I heard both sounds.

Neither required me.

That might have been the best part of the repair.

# CHAPTER 331

## THE MARKER FIELD

Antonius paid three copper to spend half a day arguing with posts.

I accepted immediately.

Not because three copper was enormous.

Because three copper for half a day was better than one copper for two hours had been, and because the work involved leaving Carrow.

Both mattered.

He found me near the lower market just after first bell.

No note.

No messenger.

Antonius himself.

That was unusual enough that I stopped before he spoke.

He wore a brown coat with mud dried to one knee and carried a rolled survey sheet under one arm.

"Free today?"

"Depends."

"On?"

"Whether you're about to ask me to do something stupid."

"Moderately stupid."

"Pay?"

"Three copper."

"How stupid?"

"Outside city. Half day. Marking old boundary posts against a current line. Mostly walking and telling me when I am about to write down the wrong thing."

"Why me?"

"Because you notice when physical things disagree with paperwork."

That was flattering in a way I distrusted.

"Who else?"

"Me. Pell. Cart driver."

"Lifting?"

"No."

"Terrain?"

"Field road. Some ditch edge. One low slope."

"Return by?"

"Before dark unless the horse joins a religion."

Reasonable.

"Three copper cash?"

"Cash."

"No debt credit?"

"Cash."

"Done."

Antonius nodded.

No negotiation.

That bothered me for six seconds.

Then I remembered I had once missed his one-copper task because I was out of town.

Maybe the market had moved.

Maybe the task was worse.

Maybe he had simply decided my time was useful.

All acceptable possibilities.

I went home long enough to tell Cala where I was going, refill water, check both crutch tips, and move the oval case deeper into the shoulder bag so it would not knock around on the road.

The holdfast stayed home.

I looked at it once.

Field work.

Unknown old posts.

A magical fixed holdfast that had demonstrated adhesion to a wooden bench.

Tempting.

No.

Untested load.

Unknown surface behavior.

Unknown release reliability.

Carrying it because `field` sounded relevant was how collections became accidents.

Separate problems.

I left it.

Antonius waited beside a narrow two-wheel cart near South Gate.

Pell sat on the back rail with a slate on his knees.

I had met him once before.

Maybe twice.

Thin, pale beard, ears that seemed designed for hearing mistakes from far away.

He looked at my crutches.

Then at Antonius.

"He walking?"

I said, "Usually."

Pell ignored me.

Antonius said, "Yes."

"All of it?"

"No. Seat between stops if needed."

Pell grunted.

Good.

Not a personality problem yet.

The cart driver was a woman named Sera.

Not first-life Sera.

Carrow Sera.

Important distinction because memory enjoyed reusing names to confuse me.

She had a wide hat and no interest in conversation.

Strong start.

We left through South Gate.

The oval clicked once in the bag.

I did not inspect it.

The city wall fell behind us.

Fields began almost immediately.

Not endless farms.

Carrow's outside edge was messier than that.

Storage yards.

Kitchen plots.

Brick cuts.

Goat pens.

Then broader grain strips divided by drainage ditches and old stone lines.

The road stayed packed earth.

The cart wheels knew every rut personally.

I sat for the first stretch.

Not pride.

Math.

If the job paid for observation, wasting my shoulders before the observation began was stupid.

Pell unrolled the survey sheet.

"Current east boundary runs from canal tooth fourteen to hill stone three. Six registered intermediate markers."

I looked at the paper.

"Registered when?"

He glanced at me.

"Twelve years ago."

"Posts older?"

"Some."

"How much older?"

"Unknown."

Antonius said, "That is why we're going."

Good.

Pell tapped the sheet.

"We are not deciding ownership. We are matching physical markers to this line and noting condition."

"So if a post disagrees?"

"We note disagreement."

"Not fix it."

"Correct."

I liked jobs with nouns that stayed in their lane.

The first marker was boring.

Excellent.

A waist-high stone post beside a ditch, square top, one face carved with a shallow hook mark.

Pell checked the sheet.

Antonius measured from the canal tooth using a cord marked at intervals.

I stood near the post and looked at it.

"What am I checking?"

Antonius said, "Everything we might regret not noticing later."

Too broad.

Pell said, "Position relative to road and ditch. Visible mark. Damage. Whether base looks moved. Anything nearby that makes the current reading questionable."

Better.

I circled the post.

No obvious fresh disturbance.

Lichen on three sides.

One side cleaner.

"South face cleaner."

Pell looked.

"Meaning?"

"Meaning south face cleaner."

He looked at me.

I smiled.

He wrote it down.

Hessa had ruined me in useful ways.

Second marker leaned.

Not much.

Maybe five degrees.

The ground around it had sunk on the ditch side.

Antonius measured.

Pell read.

"Within line tolerance."

I crouched as far as practical.

The base stone had an old crack.

Mud filled most of it.

One edge did not.

"This moved recently?"

Pell asked.

"I don't know."

"Then why ask?"

"Because one crack edge is clean."

Antonius crouched beside it.

Touched nothing.

Looked.

"Could be washout."

"Could be."

Pell wrote:

BASE CRACK / EAST EDGE CLEAN / POSSIBLE RECENT WASH

No one solved it.

Good.

Third marker was missing.

That improved the day.

The sheet said there should be a narrow iron-capped post twenty-three marked cord lengths north of the ditch bend.

There was no post.

There was a goat.

The goat seemed confident.

Pell measured twice.

Antonius checked the road bend.

Sera stayed with the horse.

I looked at the goat.

"Registered?"

Pell said, "No."

"Shame."

The goat ate something.

Maybe evidence.

We searched without searching dramatically.

No digging.

No grid.

Just walking the expected area and looking for iron, disturbed stone, old socket, fallen post.

I moved slower than they did.

That helped.

Not mystical compensation.

Just pace.

My crutch tip caught against something hard under grass.

I stopped.

Not post.

A flat stone edge.

I moved the grass aside with the crutch shaft.

Square cut.

About hand-width across.

Pell came over.

"Socket?"

"Maybe."

Antonius cleared grass with his boot.

A shallow square depression sat in the stone slab, filled with soil.

No iron post.

No broken cap.

Pell checked distance.

"Twenty-two and three quarters."

Antonius said, "Close enough to note."

I looked toward the goat.

"Questionable suspect."

The goat ignored due process.

We noted socket, no post, no conclusion.

Then moved on.

The fourth marker was where the work changed.

The road climbed a low slope beside a stand of pale grass.

At the top sat two posts.

Not one.

One stone.

One wood.

Both marked.

Both old.

Both within ten feet of the expected line.

Pell swore quietly.

Antonius said, "There it is."

"You expected this?" I asked.

"I expected something."

"Useful."

"The parcel changed hands twice in six years. The filed line stayed the same. Two neighbors now disagree which post is controlling."

There was the real job.

Not ownership.

Not adjudication.

Physical record before somebody turned memory into fact.

Pell pointed at the stone post.

"Registered description says gray stone, waist high, split crown, two-cut face."

The stone post was gray.

Waist high.

Split crown.

Two-cut face.

Easy.

The wooden post was dark oak, chest high, iron collar near base, with the same two-cut mark burned into one side.

Less easy.

"Wood newer," I said.

Pell gave me a look.

"Probably."

"Not enough."

I moved closer.

The stone post's two-cut mark was weathered almost smooth.

The wooden one was darker in the cuts but not fresh.

Antonius measured from the third expected point.

"Stone is four feet west of filed line. Wood is one foot east."

Pell said, "Filed tolerance is two."

So stone visually matched description but sat too far west.

Wood sat within tolerance but did not match material description.

Excellent.

I hated it.

We spent the next hour proving how little we knew.

Stone base had lichen down to soil.

No obvious fresh move.

Wood base showed no recent tool marks.

Iron collar older than I expected.

Maybe not six years old.

Could have been ten.

Could have been twenty.

I was not dating iron from vibes.

Pell found a second burn mark on the back of the wood.

Not the same two cuts.

Three short lines under a half circle.

I knew that mark.

Not artifact mark.

Survey crew family.

Old Greg had hired line crews before.

Road work.

Camp boundaries.

Claims after monster clearing.

The half-circle over three lines meant temporary carry-forward marker.

I thought.

Maybe.

Memory was strong enough that I felt confident.

Which meant I slowed down.

"I recognize that mark family."

Pell looked immediately.

"From where?"

Bad question.

For me.

"Old work."

"What does it mean?"

"I think temporary continuation or carry-forward. Not permanent boundary."

Antonius said, "Think?"

"Yes."

"How sure?"

I looked again.

Three lines.

Half circle.

Not closed.

One line shorter.

First life memory: a surveyor cursing because a crew had left carry-forward stakes in place after the final stones were set.

A younger me asking why anyone cared if the final line was obvious.

The surveyor saying because twenty years later nothing was obvious.

Apparently he had been right.

Annoying dead people.

"Moderately sure on category. Not sure this exact mark means the same locally."

Pell stared at me.

"Locally?"

"Marks travel. Meanings don't always."

He looked at Antonius.

Antonius said, "Note recognition as unverified."

Pell wrote:

GREG REPORTS BACK MARK RESEMBLES OLD TEMPORARY/CARRY-FORWARD SURVEY FAMILY / LOCAL MEANING UNVERIFIED

Perfect.

No one promoted me to surveyor.

We kept looking.

The wooden post had an iron collar.

Not decorative.

Set low.

Two narrow holes opposite each other.

Pell said, "Tie points?"

Antonius shrugged.

I crouched.

The ground on the east side had a shallow groove leading away through grass.

Not recent.

Old depression.

Like something had been dragged repeatedly or a cord had cut soil under tension.

Maybe livestock.

Maybe survey line.

Maybe water.

I said, "There is a groove east."

Pell wrote it.

We followed the groove twenty feet.

It vanished near a low buried stone.

That stone had no visible mark.

Antonius measured.

It sat almost exactly on the filed line.

Now we had three physical things.

Excellent.

The day was becoming professional hatred.

Pell wiped his face.

"Could be anchor."

Antonius said, "Could be field stone."

I said, "Could be where somebody tied a goat."

The goat was no longer visible.

Suspicious.

Sera called from the cart, "You done making the land worse?"

"Not yet," Antonius called.

We ate standing near the road.

Bread.

Cheese.

Water.

Mine from home.

No one bought lunch.

The oval stayed quiet.

Good object.

Pell kept looking at the wooden post while eating.

"If that back mark is temporary, wood could've been a working post set before final stone."

"Could," I said.

"Then why is it closer to filed line?"

"Because temporary crew might have been closer than whoever set the stone."

"Or the stone moved."

"Yes."

"But it doesn't look moved."

"Now."

He frowned.

Antonius said, "This is why we record before arguing."

Good Antonius.

After lunch we did something better than speculation.

We searched for corroboration.

Not the whole field.

Specific things.

If the wooden post was a temporary carry-forward, there might have been another similar temporary marker farther along the same line family.

The fifth registered marker sat beyond the slope near a dry drainage cut.

We walked there.

Stone post.

Correct description.

Within tolerance.

No wooden duplicate.

But thirty feet behind it, near a hedge, stood a cut-off oak stub with an iron collar rusted almost through.

Pell stopped.

"Well."

I said nothing.

We cleared grass around the back face.

Three short lines under a half circle.

Same family.

Closer.

Maybe exact.

Pell looked at me.

"Temporary."

"Still not proven."

"Come on."

"Two examples make a pattern. They don't write the manual."

He looked deeply offended by caution.

Hessa would have enjoyed him.

Antonius measured positions.

The oak stub sat just east of filed line.

The final stone sat nearly on it.

That supported temporary working post later replaced by stone.

At marker four, the wooden post might have been the same thing, except final stone ended up west.

Why?

Moved stone.

Bad final placement.

Changed local reference.

Filed line error.

Later replacement pretending to be original.

Too many possibilities.

We recorded all of them as possibilities by recording none of them as conclusions.

Good work was often disappointingly grammatical.

Marker six was ordinary again.

I appreciated it more.

By then my shoulders were tired.

Not failing.

Tired.

Antonius noticed before I said anything.

"Cart to last check."

I nodded.

No pride problem.

I sat.

Pell climbed up beside me.

"You actually know those marks?"

"Some family of them."

"From survey work?"

"Adjacent."

"What does that mean?"

"It means I have made enough bad decisions around people with measuring cords to remember what they yelled about."

He laughed once.

Progress.

The final check was not a marker.

Antonius wanted a sightline from hill stone three back toward canal tooth fourteen to note whether the filed route crossed an old drainage berm.

It did.

Barely.

The berm curved.

The filed line cut the inside shoulder.

Pell said, "That could explain west stone."

Antonius said, "How?"

"Crew avoiding soft berm."

"Then why file straight?"

"Because filed line is straight."

"And physical marker isn't."

"Exactly."

I said, "That explains a reason. Not whether it happened."

Pell looked at me.

"You are irritating."

"Professionally."

Antonius smiled.

We finished before fourth bell.

No horse religion.

On the ride back, I looked at the fields differently.

Not romantically.

Lines everywhere.

Fences.

Ditches.

Paths.

Old stone.

New wood.

People loved turning invisible agreements into physical objects and then pretending the objects could not lie.

Old Greg had owned land.

Lost land.

Taken land.

Paid people to tell him where land ended.

At S-class, boundaries had often been political problems wearing geography as a costume.

Here, four feet of stone mattered because somebody might spend the next ten years paying for the mistake.

Scale changed.

Human behavior did not.

The oval clicked at South Gate.

I felt it in the bag.

Ignored it.

We crossed into Carrow.

Antonius paid me near the market.

Three copper.

Cash.

He counted them into my hand.

I counted once.

Not because I distrusted him.

Because money remained money.

Five copper total now.

That was meaningful.

Not dramatic.

Meaningful.

Pell rolled the survey sheet tighter.

"If they ask again, you available?"

Antonius answered before I could.

"Depends on the task."

I looked at him.

He looked at me.

"Good answer," I said.

"I learned."

No standing job.

Good.

Pell said, "You should learn the local survey marks."

That was more dangerous.

Not because it was a job offer.

Because he was right.

"Maybe."

"I have an old reference sheet."

"Reference, not apprenticeship?"

"Gods, no."

"Excellent."

"I'll copy the mark page if I remember."

"If you remember."

"Correct."

Boundaries.

Beautiful.

I walked home with five copper and sore shoulders.

The temporary black conduit still ran along the front hall wall.

The red keep-clear line was intact.

Nobody had died while I was gone.

Strong building.

Upstairs, I put the three new copper beside the two old ones.

Five.

The number did something to the room.

Not literally.

The room remained small.

The high shelf remained high.

The holdfast remained wrapped.

The basket of mostly garbage remained mostly garbage.

But five changed options.

Mara's mark read no longer consumed everything.

Housing read no longer consumed everything.

A one-copper purchase no longer cut me in half.

Fourteen was still far.

Good.

Far was allowed.

I took out the narrow scrap.

FIELD LINE HALF DAY 3 C

I paused.

Then wrote:

5 C TOTAL

Under that:

TEMP / CARRY-FORWARD SURVEY MARK FAMILY ?

2 EXAMPLES / LOCAL MEANING NOT VERIFIED

STONE MARKER 4 FT WEST OF FILED / WOOD 1 FT EAST

DO NOT SOLVE FROM ONE MATCHING DESCRIPTION

I stared at the last line.

Too broad.

I rubbed it out.

Hessa had infected me enough already.

Then I looked at Mara's old rates written above.

MARK READ 2 C.

HOUSING 3 C.

OPEN 4 C + MATERIALS.

Five copper.

For the first time, I could pay for information and still have money afterward.

That mattered.

I looked up at the holdfast.

Then at the oval hanging near the doorway.

Two unknown pieces.

One useful enough to carry.

One still wrapped because I had never tested beyond the seller's bench.

I did not immediately grab either.

That mattered too.

Five copper was not permission to spend.

It was permission to choose.

Downstairs, Tavi shouted something about a spoon.

Lyssa shouted back that spoons did not need names.

Tavi disagreed.

The oval turned once on its cord when the upstairs doorway opened.

Click.

Normal.

I put the scrap away.

Tomorrow's problem could wait until tomorrow.

# CHAPTER 332

## THE HOUSING

Five copper was enough money to become irresponsible in more interesting ways.

I discovered this the next morning.

Not by spending it.

By realizing I could.

Two copper had made Mara's prices theoretical.

I could pay two for a mark read and have nothing left.

I could not pay three for a housing read at all.

Four plus materials had been a joke told by arithmetic.

Five changed that.

Not into affordability.

Into choice.

Which was worse.

I ate breakfast while thinking about the holdfast upstairs.

Cala noticed.

"What?"

"Nothing."

"You're chewing like money."

I stopped chewing.

"That sentence means nothing."

"It means you're counting."

"I'm eating bread."

"Expensively."

Lyssa laughed into her cup.

Tavi looked at my bread.

"Can I have expensive bread?"

"No."

Cala gave him another piece.

Economic policy collapsed immediately.

The holdfast had cost two copper.

Fixed base.

Ring.

Seller demonstration.

Unknown safe load.

Unknown surface requirement.

Unknown release behavior.

Unknown service history.

Unknown almost everything useful.

Mara's housing read cost three copper.

Five minus three left two.

That was not a comfortable reserve.

It was a reserve.

The difference mattered.

I finished breakfast.

Then did not go to Mara.

I washed the cup.

Helped Tavi find a missing strip of cloth he had put inside a boot because apparently boots were storage now.

Checked the temporary front-hall conduit with my palm near the wall for three breaths like the linewright had said.

Normal.

Went upstairs.

Looked at the holdfast.

Still there.

Very patient object.

I took out Mara's checklist.

MARK.

MATERIAL.

MOVING PARTS.

STONE OR CORE.

VISIBLE DAMAGE.

KNOWN USE.

The holdfast had a mark.

Maybe.

I had not copied it carefully enough.

Material: metal housing, dark stone or core inside ring assembly.

Moving parts: ring definitely.

Maybe internal catch.

Visible damage: wear at base edge, old scratch near rear screw.

Known use: seller fixed it to a bench and made the ring hold under a pull I had watched.

That was enough to ask a better question.

Not enough to carry it across town carelessly.

I unwrapped it without turning the ring.

The tag still read:

DO NOT TURN RING.

Good tag.

I inspected only what was already visible.

No cleaning.

No oil.

No polishing.

The mark was on the underside of the base.

I had forgotten that.

Which meant seeing it required lifting the object.

Not activating it.

Still a load problem.

I used both hands while seated, raised it only enough to slide a folded cloth under one edge, then leaned the base against the cloth without touching the ring.

Slow.

Boring.

Alive.

The mark was shallow.

Two nested hooks facing opposite directions with a short vertical cut between them.

I copied it.

Then noticed something else.

The rear screw scratch was not a scratch.

Not exactly.

A narrow line circled half the screw head.

Tool wear.

Someone had opened the housing before.

Or tried.

That mattered.

I wrote:

REAR SCREW TOOL WEAR / UNKNOWN SERVICE

Then rewrapped it.

Now I went to Mara.

The holdfast did not fit comfortably in my shoulder bag.

Of course it didn't.

I wrapped it in the ordinary sailcloth and tied the bundle to the outside of the bag with two loops, base inward, ring protected against my side.

Then hated that.

If I fell, I could land on it.

If someone hit the bag, the ring could move.

If the tie slipped, two copper could become street noise.

I untied it.

Cala watched from the doorway.

"Going somewhere?"

"Eventually."

"With that?"

"Maybe."

"You have a basket."

I looked at the repair-sweep basket.

Of course.

The remaining mundane junk came out onto the floor cloth.

Eighteen pieces.

Still eighteen.

No spontaneous treasure multiplication.

I put the wrapped holdfast in the basket.

It sat low enough that the ring did not touch the sides.

I threaded a cloth loop through the basket handle and around my right wrist.

Then picked up both crutches.

Awkward.

Not impossible.

The basket hung from my forearm, not hand.

Weight pulled wrong.

I took three steps.

Stopped.

"No."

Cala said, "Good."

"You could have said that earlier."

"You were learning."

Everyone had become Hessa.

I needed transport.

Not a cart.

Not for one object.

A strap.

Something that let the basket sit against my back or side without occupying a hand or swinging into the crutch.

I had cloth.

Lyssa had opinions.

Dangerous combination.

She looked at the basket, then at me.

"No."

"I haven't asked."

"You want me to make that carryable."

"I want to borrow a strap."

"For the thing with the ring you're not supposed to turn."

"Correct."

"No loose strap."

"Why?"

"Because it'll swing."

I knew that.

I disliked hearing it.

She took one of the older household carrying slings from a peg downstairs.

Not one of the clean gray sheets.

A wide woven band used for bundles.

She folded it through the basket handles, crossed it underneath, then tied the ends high enough that the basket would sit flat against my lower back rather than my hip.

"Try."

I did.

Better.

Not good.

Better.

The basket touched my back but did not swing.

The holdfast stayed low.

I could use both crutches.

"If it shifts?" Lyssa asked.

"Stop."

"If the ring catches?"

"Stop."

"If you fall?"

"Complain."

"Greg."

"Protect head, don't twist toward basket, then complain."

"Better."

Tavi said, "Can I carry treasure?"

Three adults said, "No."

Excellent household coordination.

Mara's shop was open.

That felt suspiciously convenient until I remembered she had told me three mornings a week if she was there.

This was apparently one of them.

A man stood at the counter holding a brass plate.

Mara was not touching it.

"You want age," she said.

"Yes."

"I can tell you what the mark supports."

"Same thing."

"No."

"Close."

"No."

I waited outside.

Good specialist.

The man eventually paid something I did not hear and left with his brass plate looking disappointed by reality.

Mara saw me.

Then the basket.

"Questions first?"

"Questions first."

"Good."

I set the basket on the floor without crossing the threshold.

The oval clicked in my shoulder bag.

Normal.

Ignored.

"I have a fixed holdfast," I said. "Bought used. Seller demonstrated one pull on a bench. I have not turned the ring since. I copied the underside mark and noticed tool wear around a rear screw. I want to know what a housing read can actually tell me before I pay for one."

Mara looked at me.

"Better."

"Than what?"

"Most people."

"Dangerous praise."

"Don't enjoy it."

She pointed at the sign.

HOUSING 3 C.

"Housing read means I inspect accessible exterior housing, visible seams, fasteners, core seat if visible without opening, wear, likely service points, and whether the housing family tells me anything supportable."

"No opening."

"No opening."

"No function claim."

"Not unless housing itself supports one."

"No safe load."

"No."

"No promise it won't hurt me."

"No."

"No activation."

"Not for three."

"Would you turn the ring?"

"Not without a reason."

Good.

"If the mark is enough for a two-copper mark read, why pay three?"

"Because your screw wear may matter more than your mark."

There it was.

I looked at the basket.

Five copper.

Three spent.

Two left.

Still able to walk away with money.

Still unable to buy anything substantial afterward.

Still enough to make another decision.

I said, "Housing read."

Mara held out her hand.

I paid three copper.

It hurt.

Not survival hurt.

Good hurt.

Money becoming information.

I had two copper left.

Mara said, "Bring it in."

I crossed the threshold.

Click.

The oval pointed back toward the door.

I ignored it.

Mara cleared a section of counter.

"Set basket there. Don't lift the object until I tell you."

I set the basket down.

She untied the carrying sling herself.

Not because she distrusted my knots.

Probably because she distrusted everyone.

Correct profession.

"Show me how it's wrapped."

I did.

She watched my hands.

"Ring hasn't moved?"

"Not since purchase."

"You sure?"

"As sure as I can be."

"Seller moved it?"
